entries.section: 1. A conversation with Nathan the prophet

paragraphs.text: 1 Now it came to pass, as David sat in his house, that David said to Nathan the prophet, “Lo, I dwell in an house of cedars, but the ark of the covenant of the LORD remaineth under curtains.” 2 Then Nathan said unto David, “Do all that is in thine heart; for God is with thee.” 3 And it came to pass the same night, that the word of God came to Nathan, saying,

entries.section: 1. A conversation with Nathan the prophet

paragraphs.text: The Lord affirms that the kingdom of David and the kingdom of Solomon are merely a share in the kingdom of God Himself, for the Lord says: “I will settle him in mine house and in my kingdom for ever” [14]. In (2 Chr 9:8) the true King of Israel is God Himself.
Our Lord directed Nathan to tell David that he was not the man chosen for this work.
Now it came to pass, as David sat in his house, that David said to Nathan the prophet,
“Lo, I dwell in an house of cedars, but the ark of the covenant of the LORD remaineth under curtains.” [1]

The book often repeats the prophecy of Nathan recorded in (2 Sam 7), and in its view it is of great importance. For it expresses the covenant made between God and David, and the continuity of his royal line, until the Son of David came, the eternal King.

David’s heart was aflame with love for God, so he could not bear to have a splendid palace while the ark of the covenant was placed in a tent. Therefore he wished to build a temple for the Lord. But everything has its own appointed time with the Lord. When David felt settled in the palace he had built, he wanted to build a house for the Lord in which the ark of the covenant would be placed. David’s mind was not at ease that he himself should dwell in a house of cedar while the ark was placed in a tent.

Look at David’s concern and his undertakings when his wealth increased and his power grew great. He did not think about what to do for his sons so as to share the wealth with them, or how to fill his treasuries and extend his authority, but rather he thought about what he might do to serve and glorify God.
Thus it is fitting for us to care for the service of the Kingdom of God in the world, and for His Church.

entries.section: 1. A conversation with Nathan the prophet

paragraphs.text: Then Nathan said unto David, “Do all that is in thine heart; for God is with thee.” [2]

As soon as Nathan the prophet learned of David’s desire, he said to him, “Do all that is in thine heart; for God is with thee,” because he had not the slightest doubt that God was with David. It is the duty of God’s servants to stir up, in themselves and in others, the movement of the grace and the gifts that are in them.

entries.section: 1. A conversation with Nathan the prophet

paragraphs.text: And it came to pass the same night, that the word of God came to Nathan, [3]

Some commentators (for example J. H. Blunt) see that Nathan the prophet’s advice was modified after the word of God came to him that night, since it is possible that the prophets were not always under divine inspiration, and could speak in some matters under the influence of their own human thought alone.

entries.section: 2. God accompanies His people wherever they are

paragraphs.text: 4 “Go and tell David my servant, Thus saith the LORD, Thou shalt not build me an house to dwell in: 5 For I have not dwelt in an house since the day that I brought up Israel unto this day; but have gone from tent to tent, and from one tabernacle to another. 6 Wheresoever I have walked with all Israel, spake I a word to any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to feed my people, saying, Why have ye not built me an house of cedars?
“Go and tell David my servant,
Thus saith the LORD, Thou shalt not build me an house to dwell in: [4]

God’s answer to David’s request came thus: David does not build this house; rather he prepares for it and does not build it, just as Moses brought the people of Israel near to Canaan, but left Joshua to bring them into it. It is the right of the Lord Christ alone to be the head of His work and the one who completes it.

entries.section: 2. God accompanies His people wherever they are

paragraphs.text: God condescends and accepts the good opinions of His people, even if He prevents them from carrying them out. He sent Nathan the prophet to comfort David’s heart and to say to him: 1. O David, your promotion to the high office was not in vain. I took you from the sheepfold, from following the sheep, not to build the temple, but to be ruler over my people Israel, and this is honor enough for you. Leave the building to another who will come after you [7]. Why should anyone think that he does everything and brings every good work to completion? Let him leave something for those who succeed him. For God gave David victories and made him a name [8], and above that He determined through him to appoint a place for His people Israel and to fortify it against its enemies; that must be his work as a man of war, and he must leave the building of churches to one who was never appointed to be a soldier. 2. O David, do not think that your good purpose has been in vain, or that you will lose its reward; for although I forbid you to carry it out, you will be rewarded as though you had done it, [for the Lord will build you an house, and will join the crown of Israel to it] [10]; for when there is a good will, it is not only accepted but also rewarded. 3. O David, do not think that I forbid you to do this great work so that it is never accomplished and that your thinking about it has been in vain; for I will raise up your seed, and he shall build me an house [11-12]. The temple of God will be built at the appointed time, even if we do not have the honor of helping to build it or the joy of seeing it completed. 4. O David, you must not confine your thoughts to the worldly prosperity of your family, but comfort yourself with the kingdom of the expected Messiah, for He is the one who comes from your loins and whose throne will be established for ever [14]. Solomon himself was not settled in the house of God as he ought to have been, and his family was not established in the kingdom: “But there shall come of your seed whom I will establish in my kingdom.” This means that he will be high priest over the house of God, and to him alone will belong authority over the works of the kingdom of God among men, and all power in heaven and on earth, in the house and in the kingdom, in the Church and in the world; so he will be a priest upon his throne, and the counsel of peace shall be between them both, and he shall build the temple of the LORD (Zech 6:12-13).

entries.section: 3. God did not ask for a house for the ark, but a tent

paragraphs.text: For I have not dwelt in an house since the day that I brought up Israel unto this day; but have gone from tent to tent, and from one tabernacle to another. [5]
The time had not yet come to set the ark in a house of the Lord.

entries.section: 3. God did not ask for a house for the ark, but a tent

paragraphs.text: Wheresoever I have walked with all Israel, spake I a word to any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to feed my people, saying, Why have ye not built me an house of cedars? [6]

God does not want outward show, pomp and splendor in His service. His ark of the covenant was content with a tent, and He did not ask for a house to be built for Him, even after God had given His people rest in great and goodly cities which they built not (Deut 6:10). He commanded the judges to feed His people, but He never asked them to build Him a house [6]. May we sometimes be content with humble comforts, as the ark of God was.

entries.section: 3. God’s pleasure in raising up leaders

paragraphs.text: Now therefore thus shalt thou say unto my servant David,
Thus saith the LORD of hosts,
I took thee from the sheepcote, even from following the sheep, that thou shouldest be ruler over my people Israel: [7]

entries.section: 3. God’s pleasure in raising up leaders

paragraphs.text: And I have been with thee whithersoever thou hast walked, and have cut off all thine enemies from before thee, and have made thee a name like the name of the great men that are in the earth. [8]
This is God’s pleasure: to raise up every human being as a leader over his feelings, thoughts, words and conduct, so that he walks in a spirit of confidence and not of fear.

St. Cyril sees that those who do not fear God are not worthy that the psalmist should mention their names with his lips [4], but God mentions the name of the poor man with His tongue (Lk 16:19, 20) [1]. He is great in the eyes of God, and God makes him great before the heavenly beings and the sons of men.

entries.section: 4. His pleasure in the rest of His people

paragraphs.text: Also I will ordain a place for my people Israel, and will plant them, and they shall be moved no more; neither shall the children of wickedness waste them any more, as at the beginning, [9]

entries.section: 5. His pleasure in building a house for those He loves

paragraphs.text: 10 And since the time that I commanded judges to be over my people Israel. Moreover I will subdue all thine enemies. Furthermore I tell thee that the LORD will build thee an house. 11 And it shall come to pass, when thy days be expired that thou must go to be with thy fathers, that I will raise up thy seed after thee, which shall be of thy sons; and I will establish his kingdom. 12 He shall build me an house, and I will stablish his throne for ever.
And since the time that I commanded judges to be over my people Israel, I will subdue all thine enemies. Furthermore I tell thee that the LORD will build thee an house [10]

Scripture says of the two midwives who refused to kill the male children of the sons of Israel: “And it came to pass, because the midwives feared God, that he made them houses” (Ex 1:21). Does God make houses?! Since the two midwives signify the Holy Bible, when it is studied with the fear of God and the believers live it as they ought, God establishes a place for the Scripture in many places; that is, the field of service opens and houses are raised up for God. Thus the world needs to see in us the word of God working in our heart with godly fear, so that the Gospel finds a place in every heart. Origen [2] sees in the two midwives “knowledge,” which supports the children of God in the birth of males as well as females, that is, in their having fruit in divine intellectual contemplation and in the sanctification of the emotions. For the males signify the intellect and the females the emotions. The two midwives also signify the Holy Bible with its two Testaments, Old and New, through which the children of God enjoy increasing fruit, intellectual and emotional, or spiritual and bodily.

entries.section: 5. His pleasure in building a house for those He loves

paragraphs.text: And it shall come to pass, when thy days be expired that thou must go to be with thy fathers, that I will raise up thy seed after thee, which shall be of thy sons; and I will establish his kingdom. [11]

entries.section: 5. His pleasure in building a house for those He loves

paragraphs.text: He shall build me an house, and I will stablish his throne for ever. [12]
Although David was obliged to enter into many battles for the stability and safety of the people, the Lord did not allow him to build the temple, because his hands had shed much blood.

entries.section: 5. His pleasure in building a house for those He loves

paragraphs.text: Who is this who builds a house for God and whose throne endures for ever, if not the Lord Christ, the Son of David, who built His Church upon the rock? Eusebius of Caesarea sees that [13] cannot apply to Solomon, but to Christ, the King of Peace.

v There is no doubt that Solomon was the son of David and his successor in the kingdom. And he was the first to build the temple of God in Jerusalem, and perhaps the Jews understand that he is the subject of the prophecy. But we rightly ask them whether the oracle applies to Solomon, which says: “I will stablish his throne for ever” [12]. And also, where did God swear with assurance by His holiness, as He foretells concerning his throne that it should be as the sun and the days of heaven?

If the years of Solomon’s reign are counted, they are forty and no more. If the years of the reign of all his descendants are added to them, they do not reach 500 years. And even if we suppose that their line (in the kingdom) continued until the last attack on the Jewish nation by the Romans, how is the prophecy fulfilled which says: “Thy throne shall remain for ever, and shall be as the sun and the days of heaven”?(*) And also the words: “I will be his father, and he shall be my son” [13].

How can they refer to Solomon? His history tells us much about him that is contrary to adoption by God and alien to it. No; hear the accusation brought against him: “But king Solomon loved many strange women, together with the daughter of Pharaoh, women of the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Zidonians, and Hittites; of the nations concerning which the LORD said unto the children of Israel, Ye shall not go in to them, neither shall they come in unto you” (1 Kgs 11:1-2).

Add to this the saying: “And his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father. For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites. And Solomon did evil in the sight of the LORD” (1 Kgs 11:4-6). Again it was said afterwards: [And the Lord raised up Satan against Solomon, Hadad the Edomite] (see 1 Kgs 11:14) LXX.

Now who can dare to say that God is the father of one who fell under such grave accusations?... Therefore we must inquire about another who is proclaimed to be of the seed of David... But there is no other born of him, as it is recorded, except our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ of God alone, who was called throughout the whole world the Son of David according to His birth in the flesh, and whose kingdom, behold, continues and will continue for ever. It has been attacked by many, but it remains always by the divine authority that surpasses humanity, to confirm that it is inspired and cannot be overcome, as the prophecy told us beforehand [3].
Eusebius of Caesarea

entries.section: 6. His pleasure in His fatherhood and mercy toward us

paragraphs.text: I will be his father, and he shall be my son: and I will not take my mercy away from him, as I took it from him that was before thee: [13]

The Apostle Paul quoted this statement(**), since he understood that it is a divine promise not to Solomon the wise as a son of David who builds the temple, but a declaration concerning the Messiah, the Son of David, in whom we enjoy adoption to the Father.

entries.section: 7. His pleasure in making us kings

paragraphs.text: But I will settle him in mine house and in my kingdom for ever: and his throne shall be established for evermore. [14]

entries.section: 7. His pleasure in making us kings

paragraphs.text: According to all these words, and according to all this vision, so did Nathan speak unto David. [15]
God gave David two promises through Nathan the prophet:
The first promise: that He will make his descendants kings of Israel [11]; this promise is conditional upon their keeping His commandments and obeying Him.

The second promise, which is unconditional: that He will raise up after him a son who will establish his throne for ever [12, 14]. This son is our Lord Jesus Christ, the incarnate Word of God, the Son of David, who establishes His kingdom in our hearts. For the Messiah in the Old Testament is the righteous eternal King, anointed to raise up the fallen tabernacle of David; His kingdom extends to the ends of the earth, and its law is truth and divine justice. Here we quote some prophecies about His wonderful person as a heavenly King and about His surpassing kingdom:
“I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth” (Jer 23:5).
“Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession” (Ps 2:8).

“Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre. Thou lovest righteousness, and hatest wickedness: therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows... Upon thy right hand did stand the queen in gold of Ophir...” (Ps 45).

“Give the king thy judgments, O God, and thy righteousness unto the king’s son. He shall judge thy people with righteousness, and thy dwellings with truth... He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth” (Ps 72).

“And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed: and the kingdom shall not be left to other people, but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever” (Dan 2:44).

“I saw in the night visions, and, behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. And there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all people, nations, and languages, should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed” (Dan 7:13-14).

v When the Lord sat on the mountain with His disciples, He saw the multitudes coming to Him, so He came down from the mountain and fed them in the lower places of the mountain. For how could He have fled there again if He had not first come down from the mountain?(***)
This carries a meaning: the Lord’s descent from on high to feed the multitudes, and His ascent...

He came now not to reign immediately, but He reigns in the sense for which we pray: “Thy kingdom come.” He reigns always with the Father as the Son of God, the Word by whom all things were made. But the prophets tell us of His kingdom in which He is the Christ who became man and makes His believers Christians...

His kingdom extends and is revealed when the glory of His saints is revealed, after the judgment has been carried out by Him, the judgment of which He spoke beforehand, which the Son of Man accomplishes. Of Him the Apostle says: [when the kingdom of God is delivered to the Father] (see 1 Cor 15:24). And He Himself indicated it, saying: [Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world] (Mt 25:34).

But the disciples and the multitudes who believed in Him thought that He had come to reign at once, and therefore they wanted to take Him by force and make Him a king (Jn 6:15). They wanted to anticipate the time which He Himself had concealed in order to reveal it at the proper time [4].
St. Augustine

entries.section: 8. David offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God

paragraphs.text: 16 And David the king came and sat before the LORD, and said, “Who am I, O LORD God, and what is mine house, that thou hast brought me hitherto? 17 And yet this was a small thing in thine eyes, O God; for thou hast also spoken of thy servant’s house for a great while to come, and hast regarded me according to the estate of a man of high degree, O LORD God. 18 What can David speak more to thee for the honour of thy servant? for thou knowest thy servant. 19 O LORD, for thy servant’s sake, and according to thine own heart, hast thou done all this greatness, in making known all these great things. 20 O LORD, there is none like thee, neither is there any God beside thee, according to all that we have heard with our ears. 21 And what one nation in the earth is like thy people Israel, whom God went to redeem to be his own people, to make thee a name of greatness and terribleness, by driving out nations from before thy people, whom thou hast redeemed out of Egypt? 22 For thy people Israel didst thou make thine own people for ever; and thou, LORD, becamest their God. 23 Therefore now, LORD, let the thing that thou hast spoken concerning thy servant and concerning his house be established for ever, and do as thou hast said. 24 Let it even be established, that thy name may be magnified for ever, saying, The LORD of hosts is the God of Israel, even a God to Israel: and let the house of David thy servant be established before thee. 25 For thou, O my God, hast told thy servant that thou wilt build him an house: therefore thy servant hath found in his heart to pray before thee. 26 And now, LORD, thou art God, and hast promised this goodness unto thy servant: 27 Now therefore let it please thee to bless the house of thy servant, that it may be before thee for ever: for thou blessest, O LORD, and it shall be blessed for ever.”
I have already given an interpretation of this prayer of David in (2 Sam 7).
And David the king came and sat before the LORD, and said,
“Who am I, O LORD God, and what is mine house, that thou hast brought me hitherto? [16]
King David met God’s answer with humility [16-18], and thanksgiving [19-20], acknowledging God’s blessings [21-22], and welcoming God’s decisions, promises and commands [23-24].

David, the prophet and king, was in a state of wonderful amazement, such that no human language can express what was within him. Although God refused that David should build Him a house, David did not grieve, but rejoiced and gave thanks, because the whole discourse points to something greater than building a house for the Lord: the Lord of glory, the Son of David, comes to raise up a house which He builds with His blood shed on the Cross.

He did not feel rejected by God because He had prevented him from building a house for God; rather he felt that he was in the divine embrace, as the Father sends the Son of David to reveal practical divine love in its most wonderful form.

David’s prayer [16-27] reveals that, although he was a man with his faults, he shows his trust in God and his dependence on Him. He emphasized that the king of Israel must not rule by his own authority, but by the power of God. For he serves a people who have entered into a covenant with God and have experience of Him.

David addressed God with awe and reverence, in answer to the message of grace he had received from God; for by faith he received the promises and embraced them and was persuaded of them, as did the patriarchal fathers (Heb 11:13).

King David sat before the Lord like a little child speaking with his father, asking of Him in the spirit of sonship. For a father delights to listen to the petition of his child. He listens to him with great attention, as one who is more pleased with his words than with the words of philosophers. Thus the saint asks of God with boldness, as a son who speaks the language of love.
A child may speak few words, but by his great love for his father he speaks with boldness and abundance, because love makes it easy for him to express what is within a person.
v The child speaks before his father with love, and his father listens with love to all that he says to him.
And when he hears the questions the child puts to him, he receives them as though he were speaking about weighty matters.
Even if he prattles much and does not distinguish what he is saying, he is more pleased with his speech than with the discourse of philosophers.
Behold, I speak like a child before his father; behold, I speak before God with great love.
Behold, I speak, though very little; yet I do not speak very little, for it is easy for love to speak much, as much as it wishes [5].
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh

entries.section: 8. David offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God

paragraphs.text: And yet this was a small thing in thine eyes, O God; for thou hast also spoken of thy servant’s house for a great while to come, and hast regarded me according to the estate of a man of high degree, O LORD God. [17]

What appears in (2 Sam) as a question, “And is this the manner of man, O Lord GOD?”, appears here in the form of a confession: “And hast regarded me according to the estate of a man of high degree, O LORD God.” You have made me a great man and have treated me as such. Through the covenant relationship that He grants to believers, God gives them titles, bestows gifts upon them, and prepares much for them, regarding them as persons of high rank although they are dust and ashes.

Some commentators read these words as follows: “You have looked upon me in the form of a man on high, O Lord GOD,” or “You have made me see, according to the form of man, the glory of the Lord GOD.” Therefore it refers to the Messiah, because David, like Abraham, saw His day and was glad; he saw it by faith, he saw Him in the form of a man, the incarnate Word, though he saw His glory as of the only begotten of the Father. And this is what God spoke concerning his house for a long time to come; this vision is, in God’s sight, greater than anything. It is not strange that David should speak of His humanity and His divinity: he called Him my Lord by the Spirit (divinity), although he knew that He would be his son (Ps 2:7; 110:1), and he saw Him made a little lower than the angels for a short time (humanity), but afterwards crowned with glory and honor (Heb 2:6-7).

When David heard of the two divine promises from the mouth of Nathan the prophet, he did not ask about particular details, nor about the time of their fulfillment; rather, in humility he stood before God, thanking Him and acknowledging His divine blessings.

entries.section: 8. David offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God

paragraphs.text: What can David speak more to thee for the honour of thy servant? for thou knowest thy servant. [18]

After the words “What can David speak more to thee,” he added here: “for the honour of thy servant” [18]. Let us note the honor that God bestows on His servants by bringing them into a covenant and fellowship with Him, to so great a degree that they can neither speak of nor desire to be honored more than that; and if they begin to think, they cannot speak of their honor more than God has spoken.
The prophet often repeats the word “thy servant,” and does so in the name of the Son of David who emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men (Phil 2:7).

entries.section: 8. David offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God

paragraphs.text: O LORD, for thy servant’s sake, and according to thine own heart, hast thou done all this greatness, in making known all these great things. [19]

It is worth noting that what is stated in (2 Sam), “for thy word’s sake,” is stated here, “for thy servant’s sake” [19]; for Jesus Christ is the Word of God (Rev 19:13) and the servant of God (Isa 42:1). For His sake the promises were given to all believers, for in Him these promises become Yea and Amen. For His sake every compassion was wrought, and for His sake it was made known; we are indebted to Him for all this greatness, and from Him we expect all these things, for they are the unsearchable riches of Christ. When we look to Him by faith, and look to the hand of the Lord Christ, we cannot but glorify, not only the great things, but the one greatest thing, which is the work and riches of Christ, and speak of it with honor.

entries.section: 8. David offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God

paragraphs.text: O LORD, there is none like thee, neither is there any God beside thee, according to all that we have heard with our ears. [20]

entries.section: 8. David offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God

paragraphs.text: And what one nation in the earth is like thy people Israel, whom God went to redeem to be his own people, to make thee a name of greatness and terribleness, by driving out nations from before thy people, whom thou hast redeemed out of Egypt? [21]

David the prophet recalls the Exodus that God accomplished by the hands of Moses and the signs and wonders that followed it, as a picture of God’s constant work with His people through the generations. Perhaps Ezra, as he records this prayer of David, links in the minds of his contemporaries God’s works in the Exodus of their fathers from Egypt with His work with them as they returned from the Babylonian captivity.
Those returning from the captivity after 70 years had in mind the picture of their fathers’ exodus from Egypt and their liberation from the slavery of Pharaoh.

entries.section: 8. David offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God

paragraphs.text: For thy people Israel didst thou make thine own people for ever; and thou, LORD, becamest their God. [22]

How humble is David, who confesses his unworthiness, and how he magnifies the name of God and marvels at His gracious condescension, and how with piety and love he magnifies the God of Israel, and what esteem he gives to Israel’s God!

entries.section: 8. David offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God

paragraphs.text: Therefore now, LORD, let the thing that thou hast spoken concerning thy servant and concerning his house be established for ever, and do as thou hast said. [23]

entries.section: 8. David offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God

paragraphs.text: Let it even be established, that thy name may be magnified for ever, saying,
The LORD of hosts is the God of Israel,
even a God to Israel: and let the house of David thy servant be established before thee. [24]

In the Second Book of Samuel it is stated, “God over Israel”(****), while here it is stated, “the God of Israel,” and He is “a God to Israel” [24]. Since He is a God to Israel, this makes clear His response to the name, His establishing of the relationship, and His doing all that they need and all that they expect of Him. There were those who were called gods of the nations, such as the gods of Assyria and Egypt, and the gods of Hamath and Arpad, but they were not gods to them, because they never stood by them at all; they were merely gods in name. But the God of Israel is a God to Israel, so all His attributes and perfections overflow for their true benefit. Blessed, and thrice blessed, is the people whose God is Jehovah, for He will be a God to them with all His attributes.

entries.section: 8. David offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God

paragraphs.text: For thou, O my God, hast told thy servant that thou wilt build him an house: therefore thy servant hath found in his heart to pray before thee. [25]

entries.section: 8. David offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God

paragraphs.text: And now, LORD, thou art God, and hast promised this goodness unto thy servant: [26]

entries.section: 8. David offers a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God

paragraphs.text: Now therefore let it please thee to bless the house of thy servant, that it may be before thee for ever: for thou blessest, O LORD, and it shall be blessed for ever. [27]

The closing words in (2 Sam 7) say: “And with thy blessing let the house of thy servant be blessed for ever,” and this is the language of holy desire, but the closing words here are the language of holy faith: [for thou blessest, O LORD, and it shall be blessed for ever] [27]. And here we see: 1. David was encouraged to ask for the blessing, because the Lord showed him that He had blessings stored up for him and for his seed: “For thou, O LORD, hast blessed me, and therefore all flesh comes to thee for the receiving of blessing; to thee I come (to receive) the blessing which thou hast promised me.” The promises were given to lead us and to stir up in us the spirit of prayer; so when God said, I will bless, let our hearts answer, Yes, Lord, bless me. 2. David was earnest in asking for the blessing, because he believed that those whom God blesses are truly blessed for ever: “Thou hast blessed, and it is blessed for ever.” Man hopes for the blessing, but God is the one who commands it; what God devises He carries out, and what He promises He does; with God, saying and doing are not two separate things. Far be it! “It is blessed for ever,” for God’s blessings are not revoked or opposed, and their benefits transcend time and days.
David ends his prayer with God’s promise of what is “for ever”; for God’s word looks to eternity, and so our desires and hopes must be.
Bless my grandchildren and my grandchildren’s grandchildren!
v David experienced Your wonderful fatherhood to him, so he longed to build You a house.
His heart found no rest after the ark of the covenant was set in the tent.
How could he rest in a palace and leave the ark in the tent?
With his pure heart, which was after Your heart, Your Spirit built a holy house in his depths.
But he was dreaming of a house for You that would befit You.
Do You, Creator of heaven and earth, dwell in houses of stone and wood?!
v Because of Your love for mankind and Your wonderful humility, You answered the request of Your beloved David.
You promised him that his son Solomon would build the house!
You counted the temple an icon of heaven and a sign of Your meeting with Your people.
v Come, O Lord Jesus, and dwell in my heart.
May Your Holy Spirit establish it, and adorn it with the spirit of holiness.
Count my heart a throne for You and a chariot like the heavenly one.
What shall I offer You that You may make Your dwelling in me?!
I have nothing to offer You but to bow down before You.
Sanctify my will, that it may be in harmony with Your will.
Lead my thoughts, my emotions and all my energy for the sake of Your Kingdom.
v To You I cry, O Lover of all mankind.
I may have children and grandchildren.
I count the whole coming generation as my children, and the generations after as my grandchildren.
I pray for the children and youth of the future.
I ask You to reveal Your love to them, that they may enter with You into a new covenant!
May they taste Your peace, Your joy and Your divine wisdom.
May they realize that You loved them before they were born!
Reveal to them Your divine presence, that they may enjoy fellowship with You.

entries.section: 1. The defeat of the Philistines

paragraphs.text: Now after this it came to pass, that David smote the Philistines, and subdued them, and took Gath and her towns out of the hand of the Philistines. [1]
David enjoyed continual victories ever since he began, as a young man, his battle with Goliath the Philistine giant, for the Lord helps him wherever he goes.

Many of the Fathers see that David’s warring against the pagan nations and his victory over them signify the work of the Lord Christ as the leader of the spiritual battle against the devil and his angels, to free us from our slavery to him and to sin.

v Christ, the true David, came to lift the human race out of the valley of sins and tears. He stood in a valley facing the Philistines (1 Sam 17:19-20). They were in a valley, because the weight of their sins pressed them down. At any rate, (the Israelites) were standing, but they did not dare to fight their adversaries.
Why did they not dare to do this? Because David, the type of Christ, had not yet arrived.

entries.section: 1. The defeat of the Philistines

paragraphs.text: This is true, beloved brethren. Who was able to fight against the devil before Christ our Lord freed the human race from his authority? Now the word David is translated “strong of hand,” and who is stronger, brethren, than the One who overcame the whole world, armed with the Cross and not with a sword?[2]
Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles. His victory over the Philistines [1]. It was already discussed in (1 Chr 14:9-16).
His victory over the Moabites [2]. This is depicted in a lesser manner than it was recorded in (1 Sam 22:3).

entries.section: 1. The defeat of the Philistines

paragraphs.text: He moved toward the north, and overcame the people of Zobah [3] and the Syrians [5].
All these nations submitted to his authority, so David reigned as far as the river Euphrates.

entries.section: 2. The defeat of the Moabites

paragraphs.text: And he smote Moab; and the Moabites became David’s servants, and brought gifts. [2]
The Second Book of Samuel (2 Sam 8:1-2) recorded for us that David killed two thirds of the Moabites, though his grandmother Ruth was a Moabitess.

entries.section: 2. The defeat of the Moabites

paragraphs.text: v It is fitting for us to recognize that those wars are a symbolic description of the victories of the Lord the Savior, since He overcame idolatry and unbelief in the whole world. These are their words that He speaks (Psalm 60), for in truth He removed their old superstitions so that they might be made fit for the change through the grace of the new man[3].

entries.section: 2. The defeat of the Moabites

paragraphs.text: Father Cassiodorus v In the Second Book of Kings (Second Samuel), where David defeated the Moabites, the Holy Bible records for us the measuring of two separate lines, one for life and the other for death (2 Sam 8:2) LXX. The meaning of leaving some of the Moabites alive while the others died is made clear through the story of Orpah and Ruth. Orpah, who returned again to idolatry and to her old city, was appointed to death. But Ruth, who followed her mother-in-law, and whose name means “Naomi (joyful),” says: “Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God” (Ruth 1:16)[4].
St. Jerome

entries.section: 3. The defeat of the Syrians

paragraphs.text: 3 And David smote Hadarezer king of Zobah unto Hamath, as he went to stablish his dominion by the river Euphrates. 4 And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen: David also houghed all the chariot horses, but reserved of them an hundred chariots. 5 And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadarezer king of Zobah, David slew of the Syrians two and twenty thousand men. 6 Then David put garrisons in Syriadamascus; and the Syrians became David’s servants, and brought gifts. Thus the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went. 7 And David took the shields of gold that were on the servants of Hadarezer, and brought them to Jerusalem. 8 Likewise from Tibhath, and from Chun, cities of Hadarezer, brought David very much brass, wherewith Solomon made the brasen sea, and the pillars, and the vessels of brass. 9 Now when Tou king of Hamath heard how David had smitten all the host of Hadarezer king of Zobah; 10 He sent Hadoram his son to king David, to enquire of his welfare, and to congratulate him, because he had fought against Hadarezer, and smitten him; (for Hadarezer had war with Tou;) and with him all manner of vessels of gold and silver and brass.
And David smote Hadarezer king of Zobah unto Hamath, as he went to stablish his dominion by the river Euphrates. [3]

Hadarezer: this name is derived from the word “Hadad,” which is the name of a Syrian god, and at one time it became the special title of the rulers of this kingdom, like “Pharaoh” for the kings of Egypt.
Zobah: near Damascus, to the northeast of it; some think that it was formerly called “Hobah” (Gen 14:15). It was the capital of the kingdom that ruled over the region of Syria.

entries.section: 3. The defeat of the Syrians

paragraphs.text: David wanted to establish his kingdom and extend it toward the Euphrates according to the divine promise (Gen 15:18; Num 24:17)[5].

entries.section: 3. The defeat of the Syrians

paragraphs.text: And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen: David also houghed all the chariot horses, but reserved of them an hundred chariots. [4]

It is stated in the Book of Deuteronomy (Deut 17:16) concerning the king, “he shall not multiply horses to himself,” lest he fall into pride, or enter into competition with the kings around him in the signs of pomp and grandeur. Therefore it seems that David kept the hundred chariots as a sign of his victory over Hadarezer and then afterwards destroyed them like the rest of the chariot horses. Some also criticize David, saying that just as he erred in polygamy (1 Chr 14:3), so here he errs in the multiplying of horses.

entries.section: 3. The defeat of the Syrians

paragraphs.text: And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadarezer king of Zobah, David slew of the Syrians two and twenty thousand men. [5]

entries.section: 3. The defeat of the Syrians

paragraphs.text: Then David put garrisons in Syriadamascus; and the Syrians became David’s servants, and brought gifts.
Thus the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went. [6]

entries.section: 3. The defeat of the Syrians

paragraphs.text: And David took the shields of gold that were on the servants of Hadarezer, and brought them to Jerusalem. [7]
David consecrated all the gold, silver and brass materials to the Lord; his son Solomon used them afterwards in building the temple.

entries.section: 3. The defeat of the Syrians

paragraphs.text: Likewise from Tibhath, and from Chun, cities of Hadarezer, brought David very much brass, wherewith Solomon made the brasen sea, and the pillars, and the vessels of brass. [8]
Tibhath and Chun: the location of these two cities is not known, nor the relationship between them. In the ancient Arabic text their names are given as Amesa (now Homs) and Baalbek.
The writer took care to stress that David took very much brass, and that Solomon made of it the brasen sea, the pillars and the vessels of brass[6].

entries.section: 3. The defeat of the Syrians

paragraphs.text: Now when Tou king of Hamath heard how David had smitten all the host of Hadarezer king of Zobah; [9]
The kingdom of Tou was on the border of the kingdom of Hadarezer (see 2 Sam 8:8-9).

entries.section: 3. The defeat of the Syrians

paragraphs.text: He sent Hadoram his son to king David, to enquire of his welfare, and to congratulate him, because he had fought against Hadarezer, and smitten him; (for Hadarezer had war with Tou).

and with him all manner of vessels of gold and silver and brass. [10] 1. It is to our advantage that our friends be among those who enjoy the divine presence. When the king of Hamath heard of the greatness of David’s success, he sent to congratulate him and to win his favor with a valuable gift [9-10].

entries.section: 3. The defeat of the Syrians

paragraphs.text: It is not profitable for anyone to oppose the Son of David; therefore “Kiss the Son, lest he be angry” (Ps 2:12). Let the kings and judges of the earth, as well as the lowly, learn and seek wisdom. The gifts we should bring to God are not vessels of gold and silver, for these befit one who has nothing to be brought to him, but we offer Him our hearts and our pure love, as well as ourselves as a living sacrifice. 2. Of the blessing that God bestows abundantly on us we must honor Him; for the gifts of his friends, like the spoils of his enemies, [David dedicated unto God] [11], that is, he kept them for building and adorning the temple, and we ought to dedicate to God, and use for the glory of His name, everything that is true and precious to us: [let our merchandise and our hire be holiness to the LORD] (Isa 23:18). 3. Those who take God with them wherever they go may expect to prosper and be preserved wherever they turn; it was said before [6] and is repeated here also [13], “Thus the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went”; God always helps those whose eyes are always turned toward Him. 4. God gives strength to men not that they may appear great with it, but that they may do good with it; when David reigned over all Israel, he executed judgment and justice among his people, and thus he responded to the result of his exaltation; he was not so focused on his victories abroad that he forgot to do justice at home, and in this he served the divine King, and God [who sitteth on the throne judging right](*), and so he was a prominent type of the Messiah, [whose sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of his kingdom](**).

entries.section: 4. The defeat of the Edomites and the dedication of the spoils to the Lord

paragraphs.text: 11 Them also king David dedicated unto the LORD, with the silver and the gold that he brought from all these nations; from Edom, and from Moab, and from the children of Ammon, and from the Philistines, and from Amalek. 12 Moreover Abishai the son of Zeruiah slew of the Edomites in the valley of salt eighteen thousand.
Them also king David dedicated unto the LORD, with the silver and the gold that he brought from all these nations;
from Edom, and from Moab, and from the children of Ammon, and from the Philistines, and from Amalek. [11]
The nations used to pay tribute to Israel because of its superiority over the nations and the strength of its authority.

David set apart for God the gifts that Tou king of Hamath sent to him, and also the gold and silver he seized as spoils from the nations, since He is the source of everything, and everything must be used for His sake.
Thus it is fitting for the believer to consecrate his heart, his gifts and his resources to God and to His glory.

entries.section: 4. The defeat of the Edomites and the dedication of the spoils to the Lord

paragraphs.text: Moreover Abishai the son of Zeruiah slew of the Edomites in the valley of salt eighteen thousand. [12]

David turned toward the south and overcame the Edomites, and occupied the Gulf of Aqaba, which opens onto the Red Sea and what lies beyond it. Solomon used it afterwards in conducting commercial relations.
The eighteen thousand whom Abishai slew were ascribed to David (2 Sam 8:13).

entries.section: 5. Garrisons set in Edom

paragraphs.text: And he put garrisons in Edom; and all the Edomites became David’s servants.
Thus the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went. [13]
The Lord gave David victory wherever he turned. David felt that God was the source of his successive victories, and did not ascribe them to his own skill, experience and personal abilities.

entries.section: 6. David’s care for justice

paragraphs.text: So David reigned over all Israel, and executed judgment and justice among all his people. [14]
As for his care for justice, King David was the head of justice. The administering of justice was the king’s responsibility (1 Kgs 3:16-28; Isa 11:4; Ps 72).
His mission as a king was to “execute judgment and justice among all his people.”
His enemies felt David’s wrath, but his people enjoyed his righteousness, his godliness and his justice. David was not only a brave and righteous leader, but also a wise administrator and organizer.

entries.section: 7. Appointments in the army and in government affairs

paragraphs.text: And Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the host; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud, recorder. [15]
The list of those who worked with him given here corresponds to what is stated in (2 Sam 8:16-18).

The second man directly after the king was Joab, the commander of the army, who entered into battles for the sake of the kingdom. Besides his command of the army he was the head of the king’s personal guard. The guarding of the king was of the utmost importance, as the cost of the fame he had gained.
Some scholars see that King David appointed a recorder after the Egyptian system, who records the events of the state.

“The recorder”: David most likely took this system from Egypt; he is like an official spokesman of the royal court, as appears in many Egyptian records, and he is nowadays close to the head of protocol.

entries.section: 8. Appointments in the service of the temple

paragraphs.text: 16 And Zadok the son of Ahitub, and Abimelech the son of Abiathar, were the priests; and Shavsha was scribe; 17 And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and the sons of David were chief about the king.
And Zadok the son of Ahitub, and Abimelech the son of Abiathar, were the priests; and Shavsha was scribe; [16]

Shavsha (Shousha) was the royal secretary, the king’s private secretary and the general secretary of state, and represents what is now the secretary of state. He was responsible for all correspondence and for the revenues of the temple, and had an important role in the general affairs of the state.
The mention of the two priests with these high leading figures in the affairs of the state reveals the strong link between the affairs of the state and the religious life of the people.

entries.section: 8. Appointments in the service of the temple

paragraphs.text: And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and the sons of David were chief about the king. [17]

It is most likely that the Cherethites and the Pelethites were a company of foreign soldiers who joined David during his flight from Saul, and remained loyal to him throughout his reign (2 Sam 15:17-18), and became part of his personal guard.

This list of military, civil and religious leaders mentions the first sons of David; in (2 Sam 8:18) it mentions them as priests, but here it mentions them as chiefs and leaders in the king’s service, since the priests had become Levites.

It is stated in (2 Sam 8:18) that “David’s sons were priests,” not for performing priestly work such as offering sacrifices, but for their carrying out some administrative work of the temple. The First Book of Chronicles made this clear, for it said that David’s sons were chief officers in the king’s service.
From Your hand come victory and success
v Despite the courage that marked David from his youth, he realized that the secret of his courage was his clinging to You.
In all his battles he does not move without You.
He hides in You, and so enjoys victory.
Grant me, in my constant battle with the devil, not to rely on past victories.
You are the secret of holiness, purity and victory.
Your grace is my support, and Your presence in my depths is the secret of my continual building up.
v Grant me, together with trust in You, to be careful to grow constantly in You.
David’s victories over the surrounding nations did not distract him from caring for his whole people and judging them with justice.
Grant me that my victory over some sins may not distract me from caring to surrender all my life to You.
Let me take shelter in Your righteousness and hold fast to Your commandments.
v His victories did not distract him from sound administration, in his army and in the affairs of the state.
Let me cling to You and enjoy wisdom and good counsel.
Then all that is within me will be under an administration worthy of Your children.
Glory to You, O Giver of victory, wisdom and counsel.
Glory to You, who care for all that is within me and all that is outside me.
You are the true Leader of all my life.

entries.section: 1. David’s consolation over Nahash, king of the children of Ammon

paragraphs.text: 1 Now it came to pass after this, that Nahash the king of the children of Ammon died, and his son reigned in his stead. 2 And David said, “I will shew kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash, because his father shewed kindness to me.” And David sent messengers to comfort him concerning his father. So the servants of David came into the land of the children of Ammon to Hanun, to comfort him.
Now it came to pass after this, that Nahash the king of the children of Ammon died, and his son reigned in his stead. [1]

The children of Ammon reached the peak of their power in the days of the judges, and David was the first military commander of the children of Israel to crush them, so they had no strength to cause trouble for Israel for many long years.

Nahash fought Israel in the days of Saul (1 Sam 11). He most likely rendered services to David in the days of Saul which were not recorded. For this reason David sent a delegation to comfort his son Hanun on the death of his father, but sadly Hanun treated them in an improper way.

entries.section: 1. David’s consolation over Nahash, king of the children of Ammon

paragraphs.text: And David said, “I will shew kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash, because his father shewed kindness to me.”
And David sent messengers to comfort him concerning his father.
So the servants of David came into the land of the children of Ammon to Hanun, to comfort him. [2]

The Holy Bible does not state what kindness Nahash showed to David, but the two entered into a close friendship during the period of David’s flight from Saul, and there was enmity between Saul and Nahash[1].
The Assyrian inscriptions state that a king of Philistia by the name of Hanun paid tribute to the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser, and that he entered into war with Sargon[2].

entries.section: 2. The counsel of the princes of the children of Ammon

paragraphs.text: 3 But the princes of the children of Ammon said to Hanun, “Thinkest thou that David doth honour thy father, that he hath sent comforters unto thee? are not his servants come unto thee for to search, and to overthrow, and to spy out the land?” 4 Wherefore Hanun took David’s servants, and shaved them, and cut off their garments in the midst hard by their buttocks, and sent them away. 5 Then there went certain, and told David how the men were served. And he sent to meet them: for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, “Tarry at Jericho until your beards be grown, and then return.”
But the princes of the children of Ammon said to Hanun,
“Thinkest thou that David doth honour thy father, that he hath sent comforters unto thee?
are not his servants come unto thee for to search, and to overthrow, and to spy out the land?” [3]

When David rebuked Saul because he listened to his wicked counselors who were stirring him up against David unjustly, David said to him: “As saith the proverb of the ancients, Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked” (1 Sam 24:13). This is what King Hanun fell into, for he set up for himself wicked counselors, and they offered them out of what they had, which is evil. It is fitting for leaders not to incline their ears to the counsels of the wicked. It was fitting for the king not to think ill; together with wisdom and caution, it is fitting for us not to be hasty in thinking ill of others.

entries.section: 2. The counsel of the princes of the children of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Wherefore Hanun took David’s servants, and shaved them, and cut off their garments in the midst hard by their buttocks, and sent them away. [4]

Shaving the beard, especially a part of it, and tearing the garments in the middle, for someone against his will, was considered among the Jews and among Easterners in general a grave insult, a severe contempt and a challenge.
This view still exists in Egypt to this day, especially in the villages.

entries.section: 2. The counsel of the princes of the children of Ammon

paragraphs.text: Then there went certain, and told David how the men were served.
And he sent to meet them: for the men were greatly ashamed.
And the king said, “Tarry at Jericho until your beards be grown, and then return.” [5]

David the prophet presents to us a wonderful example of leaders who care for the dignity of those who work with them and carry out the service. He sent to meet them, because they were in shame, unable to meet anyone. He met them to raise their morale and to support them.

If David cared for those who worked with him so that no harm would befall them, how much more does the Lord of David care for His servants who suffer troubles and pains. If they accept crucifixion with Him with all joy, He grants them the power of the Resurrection, its joy and its glory.

entries.section: 3. Hanun hires an army from Syria

paragraphs.text: 6 And when the children of Ammon saw that they had made themselves odious to David, Hanun and the children of Ammon sent a thousand talents of silver to hire them chariots and horsemen out of Mesopotamia, and out of Syriamaachah, and out of Zobah. 7 So they hired thirty and two thousand chariots, and the king of Maachah and his people; who came and pitched before Medeba. And the children of Ammon gathered themselves together from their cities, and came to battle. 8 And when David heard of it, he sent Joab, and all the host of the mighty men. 9 And the children of Ammon came out, and put the battle in array before the gate of the city: and the kings that were come were by themselves in the field.

And when the children of Ammon saw that they had made themselves odious to David, Hanun and the children of Ammon sent a thousand talents of silver to hire them chariots and horsemen out of Mesopotamia, and out of Syriamaachah, and out of Zobah. [6]
The story in this chapter concerning the alliance between the children of Ammon and the Syrians, and the victory over them, is found in (2 Sam 10).
Hanun king of Ammon and his counselors thought ill of David’s intentions, and so brought a disaster upon themselves, their country and the countries neighboring them.
Instead of Hanun’s acknowledging his rashness and folly in his conduct, he devoted a huge sum (a thousand talents of silver) to cover his error by entering into a failed battle.

Instead of David’s being the one who wanted war, it was the new king of the Ammonites who wanted this, and therefore he hired an army from Syria to help him against David, and we see here: 1. How the hearts of the wicked are hardened for their destruction, for the children of Ammon, when they saw that they had made themselves odious to David [1]. Instead of seeking peace and correcting what they had done, humbling themselves and seeking to satisfy David for the harm they had committed, behold, not only had they made themselves odious to David, but they also hated the justice of God, who is “King of nations,” who defends the right of the oppressed and keeps the violated laws of nations; indeed, they prepared for war and brought destruction upon themselves at the hands of David, which he had not intended for them. 2. How the courage of brave men increases in distress, for “when Joab saw that the battle was set against him before and behind” [10], instead of thinking of retreat he redoubled his resolve, and although he could not double his army, he divided it, and he did not merely speak but acted, as a gallant man of great presence of mind; and when he saw himself surrounded, he agreed with his brother that each should help the other [12], and urged himself and his soldiers to act strongly, each in his position, with the aim of the glory of God and the good of their country, and not their own honor and personal benefit, and they left the matter to God: “and let the LORD do that which is good in his sight” [13]. 3. How the greatest arts of war that are aimed against justice and equity avail nothing, for the children of Ammon did all in their power to strengthen their position; they brought a mighty force into the field of battle and used it cunningly to the extent of their ability, yet because they were in the wrong and were defending falsehood, all this did not profit, and they were conquered in the most notorious defeat; for truth always prevails and triumphs in the end.

entries.section: 3. Hanun hires an army from Syria

paragraphs.text: So they hired thirty and two thousand chariots, and the king of Maachah and his people;
who came and pitched before Medeba.
And the children of Ammon gathered themselves together from their cities, and came to battle. [7]
The children of Ammon hired 32,000 chariots and also horsemen experienced in fighting with chariots, and also some infantry whom the text does not mention.

entries.section: 3. Hanun hires an army from Syria

paragraphs.text: And when David heard of it, he sent Joab, and all the host of the mighty men. [8]
David sent Joab and his brother Abishai with all the military forces against the forces of the children of Ammon allied with the Syrians, and they were victorious over them.

entries.section: 3. Hanun hires an army from Syria

paragraphs.text: And the children of Ammon came out, and put the battle in array before the gate of the city: and the kings that were come were by themselves in the field. [9]
The army of the children of Ammon set out and drew up in array at the gate of the city, that is, outside the walls opposite Medeba on the border of the city of Arnon.

The Israelite army was alarmed by the Ammonites who were in front, and behind them the hired Syrian mercenaries. Joab determined to resist the mercenaries, and asked his brother Abishai to attack the Ammonites.
When the mercenaries were defeated, the courage of the Ammonites failed, and they were forced to flee[3].

paragraphs.text: 10 Now when Joab saw that the battle was set against him before and behind, he chose out of all the choice of Israel, and put them in array against the Syrians. 11 And the rest of the people he delivered unto the hand of Abishai his brother, and they set themselves in array against the children of Ammon. 12 And he said, “If the Syrians be too strong for me, then thou shalt help me: but if the children of Ammon be too strong for thee, then I will help thee. 13 Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the LORD do that which is good in his sight.” 14 So Joab and the people that were with him drew nigh before the Syrians unto the battle; and they fled before him. 15 And when the children of Ammon saw that the Syrians were fled, they likewise fled before Abishai his brother, and entered into the city. If in the days of Saul none stood before Goliath the giant except the youth David the hero, now in the age of David there were many heroes standing before the giants of the hostile nations.
