paragraphs.text: And the rest of the people he delivered unto the hand of Abishai his brother, and they set themselves in array against the children of Ammon. [11]

entries.section: 4. The defeat of the Syrian allies

paragraphs.text: And he said, “If the Syrians be too strong for me, then thou shalt help me: but if the children of Ammon be too strong for thee, then I will help thee. [12]

entries.section: 4. The defeat of the Syrian allies

paragraphs.text: Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the LORD do that which is good in his sight.” [13]

The secret of the success of Joab and his brother Abishai is that, while studying the situation with all seriousness and arranging the matter, they were confident in God to do what was for the good of the people: “let the LORD do that which is good in his sight” [13].
On the other hand, Joab supported his brother, urging him: “Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God.”

And it is remarkable that while they take pride in the people, ascribing them to themselves, “our people,” at the same time they ascribe the cities to God, “the cities of our God.” On the one hand they want to affirm their love for the people, and on the other hand God is the guardian of the people and their shepherd.

entries.section: 4. The defeat of the Syrian allies

paragraphs.text: So Joab and the people that were with him drew nigh before the Syrians unto the battle; and they fled before him. [14]

As Joab’s speech to his brother Abishai revealed their love for the people and their trust in the Lord, the enemy collapsed before them. Nothing shatters the power of the enemy of good like love for God and for the brethren. Therefore it is fitting for the believer, whether priest or of the people, to adorn himself or arm himself with love, so that the powers of darkness cannot prevail against him. By true love we fear neither the lusts of the flesh nor the lust of the love of the world, nor the devil and all his powers.
This love for God and for the brethren cannot be separated.
v He who fixes his mind on the love of God despises all things visible, even his own body becomes a stranger to him.

v He who sees a trace of hatred in his heart toward any man, through any fault whatever, makes himself altogether a stranger to the love of God, for the love of God cannot in any way cleave to hatred of man.
v Blessed is the man who learns to love all men equally.

v If you hate some people, and others you neither hate nor love, and some you love a little, and others you love much, you need to know from this variety in love that you are very far from perfect love, one of whose pillars is equality in love.
v He who loves God certainly loves his neighbor also. Such a person cannot hold fast to money, but rather, like God, gives it to everyone in need.

v When the mind begins to advance in the love of God, the demon of blasphemy begins to fight against it, suggesting to it strange, demonic thoughts; this happens because he bears a grudge against the new friend of God. And when the person thinks these thoughts about God, he feels shame and disgrace, and as a result he cannot draw near to God and pray. But by the power of God we gain the victory over him, and prevail over his wicked way, and are strengthened, and become more sincere in our love for Jesus. [His sword shall enter into his own heart, and his bows shall be broken] (Ps 37:15).
Father Maximus the Confessor[4]
v O the greatness of love! Stronger than fire itself, it ascends to heaven itself, and there is none to hinder it[5].
v Paul, a citizen of heaven, a pillar of the Church, an earthly angel, a heavenly being. Like iron heated by fire becomes all aglow, so Paul was set aflame with love and became love itself[6].
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 4. The defeat of the Syrian allies

paragraphs.text: And when the children of Ammon saw that the Syrians were fled, they likewise fled before Abishai his brother, and entered into the city.
Then Joab came to Jerusalem. [15]

When Joab was victorious, his brother Abishai took courage and was victorious also. So if our sins cause our brethren to stumble, so that we are the cause of their fall, then our victory in the Lord supports our brethren so that they are strengthened and cleave to the Lord and are victorious with us!
With every victory you enjoy, you support your brother that he too may be victorious by God, his God.

entries.section: 4. The defeat of the Syrian allies

paragraphs.text: And when the Syrians saw that they were put to the worse before Israel, they sent messengers, and drew forth the Syrians that were beyond the river: and Shophach the captain of the host of Hadarezer went before them. [16]

The Syrians sent to their kinsmen beyond the river and planned to take revenge on Israel. When David quickly realized the danger, he gathered his forces and took a defensive position. The arrogance of the Syrians fell, and they became servants to David.

entries.section: 4. The defeat of the Syrian allies

paragraphs.text: And it was told David; and he gathered all Israel, and passed over Jordan, and came upon them, and set the battle in array against them.
So when David had put the battle in array against the Syrians, they fought with him. [17]

It seems in this chapter that David was sharp in temper, but he tried to live in peace. And we note here: 1. It is the disposition of godly people to be good neighbors, and especially to be thankful; David wanted to show kindness to Hanun as a neighbor, and because he remembered his father’s kindness to him; for those who receive kindness must repay it according to their ability when the opportunity arises, and those who receive from fathers must repay the sons after their departure. 2. It is “as saith the proverb of the ancients, Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked” (1 Sam 24:13); “for the vile person will speak villany... The instruments also of the churl are evil... to destroy... with lying words, even when the needy speaketh right” (Isa 32:6-7). So these lowly men who devise evil by themselves tend to jealousy and to thinking ill of others without cause. Hanun’s servants advised him that David’s messengers had come to spy out the land, as if a great man like David needed to do something mean like this; for if he had an evil intention against the Ammonites, he could have carried it out by force and not resorted to a base method; yet Hanun yielded to the opinion of his servants and, against the laws of nations, treated David’s messengers in a vile manner.

The children of Ammon were enemies of Israel, but David did not want to make war; he was on the defensive, as was the case with him for most of his life, for the man of God always finds himself on the defensive; we must put on the whole armor of God. What does this mean? Is it so that we may advance to war? No, but that we may stand ready, and this is what matters. 3. Leaders must protect their servants, and care for and attend to their affairs if harm befalls them in their service; David did so for his messengers [5], and the Lord Christ does likewise for His servants.

entries.section: 4. The defeat of the Syrian allies

paragraphs.text: But the Syrians fled before Israel; and David slew of the Syrians seven thousand chariots and forty thousand footmen, and killed Shophach the captain of the host. [18]

Those with whom God is not gather their strength again without the slightest profit; the Syrians had no interest in the matter at all, and served with the children of Ammon as mercenary soldiers, and when they were struck they thought of regaining their honor, and therefore sought help from the Syrians on the other bank of the Euphrates, but in vain, for they [fled before Israel] [18]. They lost seven thousand men, of whom it was said that they were men of seven hundred chariots (2 Sam 10:18).

entries.section: 5. The submission of Hadarezer’s leaders to David

paragraphs.text: And when the servants of Hadarezer saw that they were put to the worse before Israel, they made peace with David, and served him.
Neither would the Syrians help the children of Ammon any more. [19]

When the Syrians saw that Israel was the victor, they broke their alliance with the children of Ammon, “neither would the Syrians help the children of Ammon any more” [19], and also made peace with David and became his servants. If only those who have stood in vain against God would return to themselves [and be reconciled to Him quickly while they are in the way] (Mt 5:25), and become His servants, for they have made themselves negligent if they become His enemies.
Grant me to flee from the counsel of the wicked
v From the wicked proceeds wickedness; protect me from them, that I may not incline my ear to them, but incline my ear to Your life-giving commandment.
v Because of the counsel of the wicked, Hanun the son of Nahash lost David’s friendship.
Instead of allying himself with David, so that the blessing of the Lord would come upon him, the evil of the wicked came upon him, and he paid for this a cost of this amount!
He lost his money, his chariots and his dignity.
v Hanun and his men insulted David’s messengers, so they hid in shame.
David, the man of the wide heart, cared with humility.
By his love, concern and care, he lifted their spirits.
And he did not allow any of his people to see them, so that no one would mock them.
v O Lord of David, all-loving, tender and kind.
Look upon Your servants and Your people.
You permit for a time the hand of the wicked to be stretched out against them.
But do not allow this hand to rest upon them.
Instead of mockery, pour out Your splendor upon them.
And instead of shame, reveal Your glory in them.
v Joab and his brother Abishai were strengthened to work on behalf of the Lord.
They trusted in God, so their lives were filled with strength, courage and hope.
And victory truly became their ally.
v Their wonderful love for their people was blended with God’s care for the people.
They took pride in the people, and called them “our people”!
They carried the people, as it were, on their hands before God, and so they realized God’s guarding of His people and the protection of their cities!

entries.section: 1. David compels Joab to number the people

paragraphs.text: 1 And Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel. 2 And David said to Joab and to the rulers of the people, “Go, number Israel from Beersheba even to Dan; and bring the number of them to me, that I may know it.” 3 And Joab answered, “The LORD make his people an hundred times so many more as they be: but, my lord the king, are they not all my lord’s servants? why then doth my lord require this thing? why will he be a cause of trespass to Israel?” 4 Nevertheless the king’s word prevailed against Joab. Wherefore Joab departed, and went throughout all Israel, and came to Jerusalem. 5 And Joab gave the sum of the number of the people unto David. And all they of Israel were a thousand thousand and an hundred thousand men that drew sword: and Judah was four hundred threescore and ten thousand men that drew sword. 6 But Levi and Benjamin counted he not among them: for the king’s word was abominable to Joab.
And Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel. [1]

Who was behind this sin? It is written in (2 Sam 24:1): “the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he moved David against them to say, Go, number Israel and Judah.” It is as though the Lord urged David to do it, because His anger had come upon the people. In the Book of Chronicles it is said that Satan was behind this act. Both are true, for God permitted Satan to tempt David. God is not the source of evil, but He permits it to accomplish His purposes. Satan offers the temptation, but he does not compel man to accept it.

It is evident here that Satan does not stand idly by before God’s plan and His continual works for accomplishing salvation. He tempted David’s heart in order to scatter God’s plans for His people. Satan tempted him as the serpent tempted Eve and Adam, and he also tried to tempt Job in order to destroy him (Job 1-2), and Zechariah the prophet saw him in one of the visions he beheld (Zech 3:1).

Numbering the people is not evil in itself, since it is fitting for a shepherd to know his flock. But it is clear that David sinned in this act and was the cause of God’s anger, because he did this out of pride of heart and lack of trust in God, relying on numbers. David carried out this census in order to boast of the strength of his army, to rely on his military capabilities rather than on God. The motive for his act was sin, namely vanity. Often sin lies not in our outward actions, but in our hidden motives.

We are certain that God does not cause sin, for “neither tempteth he any man.” Therefore, when it is said that He moved David to do it, it must be made clear that for a wise and holy purpose God permitted Satan to do it, and here we trace this erroneous course to its source and foundation. It is not strange that Satan, who is the enemy of God and of everything good, should stand against the people; for his aim is to destroy David and the people. Here we notice the following: 1. It is astonishing that Satan influences David to do something wrong, he who was a man whose heart was like God’s heart, for it would be supposed that he was among those whom the wicked one does not touch. God permitted this so that we may know that the holiest of the saints must not think that they are beyond the reach of Satan’s temptations. This reminds us of St. Macarius the Great, to whom Satan said, “You have arrived, O Macarius,” and he kept answering him, “I have not arrived,” until he gave up his spirit into the hand of his Creator, and then he said, “Now I have arrived.” Now when Satan intended to bring harm upon Israel, what way did he take? He did not [stir up God against them to swallow them up] (Job 2:3), but he stirred up David, their dearest friend, to number them, and thereby to anger God and provoke Him against them. 2. When Satan tempts us to sin against God, he harms us more than by his complaint against us before God. He destroys people by their own selves and their own hands. 3. The greatest harm Satan can do to the Church of God is to tempt its leaders with pride, because no one can see this sin in everyone, and especially in those who are foremost in the Church: “But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve” (Lk 22:26).
v David believed in You, and You took him from behind the sheep, and made him king, and he triumphed over Goliath and subdued all his persecutors.
The devil stirred up his forces against him from every side, but because Your right hand held his hand, he persevered and received courage.
The wicked one put it into his heart to number the nation, so the Lord disciplined him with mercy and received him with love (2 Sam 24).
He made him king, and filled him with the spirit of prophecy, and the wealth of his words overflowed and filled all creation.

entries.section: 1. David compels Joab to number the people

paragraphs.text: He became a fountain, from which the words of the Holy Spirit burst forth, and the peoples and the worlds drank from it, and they are still thirsty for them [2].
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh

entries.section: 1. David compels Joab to number the people

paragraphs.text: And David said to Joab and to the rulers of the people,
“Go, number Israel from Beersheba even to Dan; and bring the number of them to me, that I may know it.” [2]

entries.section: 1. David compels Joab to number the people

paragraphs.text: And Joab answered, “The LORD make his people an hundred times so many more as they be:
but, my lord the king, are they not all my lord’s servants?
why then doth my lord require this thing?
why will he be a cause of trespass to Israel?” [3]

This story highlights David’s fall into a weakness that no one expected, which led Joab to rebuke David for it. David sinned because he relied on the arm of his people, contrary to his custom, and sought the glory of himself.

The Lord Himself had warned him when He said to him by the mouth of Nathan the prophet: [I was with thee whithersoever thou hast walked, and have cut off all thine enemies from before thee, and have made thee a name like the name of the great men that are in the earth] (1 Chr 17:8).

David did not consult God before carrying out the census, nor did he heed Joab’s advice. For Joab was against the idea of taking a census, and did not take the order David issued in this matter seriously.

Joab, whom David used, was a man of standing in public affairs, but he was compelled to this task, and did it with the utmost reluctance imaginable. He lodged a protest against this work before he began it, for there was no man more advanced than he in anything that tended to the glory of the king and the good of the kingdom, but in this matter he wished gladly to be excused, for two reasons: 1. He saw that there was no need for it and no occasion for it, for God had promised to multiply His people, and Joab had no question about the fulfillment of this promise; all the people were the king’s servants and he had no doubt of their loyalty and love for him. 2. This matter was dangerous, and carrying it out might cause a trespass for Israel and perhaps stir up God’s anger against them. Joab understood this, but David did not understand it, so consultation in a spirit of humility was necessary.

entries.section: 1. David compels Joab to number the people

paragraphs.text: Nevertheless the king’s word prevailed against Joab.
Wherefore Joab departed, and went throughout all Israel, and came to Jerusalem. [4]

He was troubled by this matter before he undertook it: “for the king’s word was abominable to Joab.” Everything King David had done before this was good in the eyes of all the people (2 Sam 3:36), but now there was a general aversion to these orders, which confirmed Joab’s hatred of them.

entries.section: 1. David compels Joab to number the people

paragraphs.text: And Joab gave the sum of the number of the people unto David. And all they of Israel were a thousand thousand (a million) and an hundred thousand men that drew sword: and Judah was four hundred threescore and ten thousand men that drew sword. [5]

Although the result of this review was very great, Joab had no heart to complete it, and he left two important tribes without being numbered, namely the tribes of Levi and Benjamin [5-6]. Perhaps he was not careful in numbering the other tribes, because he did the work grudgingly, which explains the difference between the figures of the census and what is recorded in (2 Sam 24:9).

The difference in the figures of the census here and in (2 Sam 24) is due to the fact that 2 Samuel does not count the standing army mentioned in (1 Chr 28), which also adds the captains of hundreds and the captains of thousands. For David did not want to know the number of the regular army, since he knew it well in general terms, but he wanted to know the extent to which the strength of Israel could reach, so that he might use it on any possible occasion.

entries.section: 1. David compels Joab to number the people

paragraphs.text: But Levi and Benjamin counted he not among them: for the king’s word was abominable to Joab. [6]

The tribe of Levi was not numbered because they are not subject to compulsory conscription, and because the tribe was scattered among the rest of the tribes, and it was difficult to gather the number of the Levites. Benjamin was not numbered, because the census was disrupted before reaching Benjamin (1 Chr 27:24), on account of the spread of the plague.

There is a great contrast between this incident and what happened to David the young shepherd when he came to the field of battle and saw Goliath the giant strutting about arrogantly and taunting Israel. That little shepherd did not wish to take a census and did not number the army, but it is written in his psalms: “It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man. It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in princes” (Ps 118:8-9). He said, [Let me face him](*). Why did he have the courage to do so? Because he trusted in the Lord. And he learned the lesson from the incident of the census.

v Great is the power of hope in the Lord: an unconquerable fortress, a protecting wall that cannot be attacked, a military reinforcement that is not defeated, a quiet harbor, a strong tower, an irresistible weapon, an unconquerable strength able to find a refuge in a place no one expects. By this power the unarmed become armed, the condition of women becomes better than that of men, and children prove that they easily become stronger than those who practice the arts of war. What wonder is it if they overcome enemies, when in reality they overcome the world itself?... Hope in the Lord changes everything! [3]

v He did not say, “I shall not suffer,” but “I will not fear what man shall do unto me,” meaning that although I suffer, I do not fear, as Paul also said: “If God be for us, who can be against us?” (Rom 8:31). In reality there were countless things against him, but he did not use them wrongly... He was higher and loftier above all fears...
God loves you, my dear ones, and therefore He draws you away from everything... and pulls you to Himself [4].

St. John Chrysostom v They say: Why does (divine providence) not support you when you are persecuted?... What evil can befall us as long as we look to death as a departure, by which we go to the Lord, as though it were a change of life, we pass from one life to another life?!...

Each of us says with confidence: [The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me?] (Ps 118:6). [But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and there shall no torment touch them] (Wis 3:1)... They persecute us not because we are evildoers, but they think that we Christians sin against life, and that we act against ourselves [5].

St. Clement of Alexandria v Before the war begins, seek an ally; before falling ill, let you have your physician; before sorrowful things come upon you, pray, for in the time of your sorrows you will find Him, and He will hear you [6].

Mar Isaac the Syrian And we must ask ourselves this important question: Do we always believe and trust in the Lord? “But without faith it is impossible to please him...” (Heb 11:6). And the Lord Jesus, glory be to Him, said: [When the Holy Spirit is come, he will reprove the world of sin]. What sin...? “Because they believe not on me” (Jn 16:8-9), and St. Paul the Apostle said: “For whatsoever is not of faith is sin” (Rom 14:23). This was David’s sin in that incident, and he soon realized the extent of the error into which he had fallen in this matter.

entries.section: 2. David’s repentance for what he had done

paragraphs.text: 7 And God was displeased with this thing; therefore he smote Israel. 8 And David said unto God, “I have sinned greatly, because I have done this thing: but now, I beseech thee, do away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly.”
And God was displeased with this thing; therefore he smote Israel. [7]
In the census the ransom commanded in (Ex 30:12) was not collected. And David’s pride and disobedience brought grave consequences.

v The conduct of rulers is often tied to the characteristics of those subject to them, so that even those who are truly good shepherds sin as a result of the evil of their flock. For David the prophet, who was praised by the testimony of God Himself, and who was qualified to know heavenly mysteries, was puffed up with sudden pride, and sinned by numbering the people. And although it was he who sinned, the people fell under the punishment. Why? Because in truth the hearts of rulers are affected by the deserts of their peoples.
The godly judge (David) was rebuked for the sinner’s error by having a punishment imposed on the very persons on whose account he himself had sinned...

Since he fell into pride with full freedom of his will, he fell under punishment for his sin. For this severe wrath that struck the people in their bodies wore down the ruler of the people with pain in the depths of his heart. Surely the deserts of rulers and people are shared and interlinked, since the conduct of the people often becomes evil because of the error of their shepherds, and the conduct of the shepherds changes according to the deserts of their people [7].
Father Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 2. David’s repentance for what he had done

paragraphs.text: And David said unto God, “I have sinned greatly, because I have done this thing.
but now, I beseech thee, do away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly.” [8]
When David realized his sin and its gravity, he took responsibility, and was quickly broken, confessing his error before the Lord and asking Him to forgive him.

He confessed his sin sincerely and prayed for its forgiveness [8]. He confessed that he had sinned greatly, and that he had done this thing very foolishly, and he besought that the iniquity be removed.

v When David ordered the numbering of the people, he was greatly smitten in his heart, and said: [I have sinned greatly, because I have done this thing: but now, I beseech thee, O LORD, do away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly] (see 1 Chr 21:8). And Nathan the prophet was sent (to him) again to choose (one of the chastisements)... David said that these three (chastisements) are great calamities for me, but I fall into the hand of the Lord, for His mercies are very great, and I do not fall into the hands of men.
David’s error was that he desired to know the numbers of all the people who were with him; this knowledge should have been left to God alone.

It is said that when the plague came upon the people on the first day at supper time, David, seeing the angel smiting the people, said: [I the shepherd have sinned, and have done evil, but these sheep, what have they done? Let thine hand be on me, and on my father’s house]. Then the Lord repented, and commanded the angel to spare the people, and that David should offer a sacrifice, since sacrifices at that time were offered for sin, but now they are sacrifices of repentance. Thus by his humility he became more acceptable to God. For it is not strange that men should err, but they deserve rebuke if they do not know that they have sinned and so do not humble themselves before God [8].
St. Ambrose

entries.section: 3. The choice of chastisement

paragraphs.text: 9 And the LORD spake unto Gad, David’s seer, saying, 10 “Go and tell David, saying, Thus saith the LORD, I offer thee three things: choose thee one of them, that I may do it unto thee.” 11 So Gad came to David, and said unto him, “Thus saith the LORD, Choose thee 12 Either three years’ famine; or three months to be destroyed before thy foes, while that the sword of thine enemies overtaketh thee; or else three days the sword of the LORD, even the pestilence, in the land, and the angel of the LORD destroying throughout all the coasts of Israel. Now therefore advise thyself what word I shall bring again to him that sent me.” 13 And David said unto Gad, “I am in a great strait: let me fall now into the hand of the LORD; for very great are his mercies: but let me not fall into the hand of man.”
And the LORD spake unto Gad, David’s seer: [9]

entries.section: 3. The choice of chastisement

paragraphs.text: “Go and tell David, saying, Thus saith the LORD,
I offer thee three things: choose thee one of them, that I may do it unto thee.” [10]

entries.section: 3. The choice of chastisement

paragraphs.text: So Gad came to David, and said unto him,
“Thus saith the LORD, Choose thee [11]

entries.section: 3. The choice of chastisement

paragraphs.text: Either three years’ famine; or three months to be destroyed before thy foes, while that the sword of thine enemies overtaketh thee; or else three days the sword of the LORD, even the pestilence, in the land, and the angel of the LORD destroying throughout all the coasts of Israel.
Now therefore advise thyself what word I shall bring again to him that sent me.” [12]

David fell under the rod of chastisement because of the numbering of the people. This rod of chastisement drives foolishness out of the heart, the foolishness of pride and of relying on numbers instead of trusting in God, and let us consider the following: 1. David realized that this thing was evil in the eyes of God [9-11], and this is no light matter for a good man like David. The Lord looks and takes no pleasure in the sin of His people, and there is no sin more displeasing to God than pride of heart and lack of trust in God; likewise nothing is more grievous and deadly to a sensitive soul than to be an object of God’s displeasure.

It is profitable for us to notice how God focuses on certain things in David’s life, for many here consider that some attitudes are sin and other attitudes are not sin or are less wrong, but when we stand in God’s presence we shall discover that our view was mistaken in this respect, and we shall know the meaning of sin. We must know that sin is not only in deeds, that is, the things we do or do not do, but also in thoughts and intentions, and by studying the word of God we know His view of sin. 2. David was given the choice of one punishment out of three: war, famine, or pestilence, and thereby God permits him to be humbled for the sake of his repentance and the salvation of his soul all the more; he was placed in a very difficult position before the dread of three punishments, without doubt amid his great bewilderment when he considered which of the three to choose.

entries.section: 3. The choice of chastisement

paragraphs.text: And David said unto Gad, “I am in a great strait:
let me fall now into the hand of the LORD; for very great are his mercies: but let me not fall into the hand of man.” [13]
When the opportunity to choose the chastisement was offered to him, he preferred falling into the hand of the Lord to falling into the hand of man, because he knew that He is merciful.

entries.section: 4. The pestilence and the deliverance of Jerusalem from it

paragraphs.text: 14 So the LORD sent pestilence upon Israel: and there fell of Israel seventy thousand men. 15 And God sent an angel unto Jerusalem to destroy it: and as he was destroying, the LORD beheld, and he repented him of the evil, and said to the angel that destroyed, “It is enough, stay now thine hand.” And the angel of the LORD stood by the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite. 16 And David lifted up his eyes, and saw the angel of the LORD stand between the earth and the heaven, having a drawn sword in his hand stretched out over Jerusalem. Then David and the elders of Israel, who were clothed in sackcloth, fell upon their faces. 17 And David said unto God, “Is it not I that commanded the people to be numbered? even I it is that have sinned and done evil indeed; but as for these sheep, what have they done? let thine hand, I pray thee, O LORD my God, be on me, and on my father’s house; but not on thy people, that they should be plagued.”
So the LORD sent pestilence upon Israel: and there fell of Israel seventy thousand men. [14]
Sin has a chain effect, for it drags behind it a series of consequences. When we remember the consequences that will come upon us, sin becomes bitter in our mouth and we reject it.

Within a few hours David heard of the fall of seventy thousand of his subjects, who died by the pestilence. He had been proud of the abundance of his people, but the divine chastisement took its course to make them fewer in number; for justly that in which we boast is taken from us, so that we fall into weakness and feel its bitter taste. David had insisted on numbering his people and said: “Go, number Israel... and bring the number of them to me, that I may know it” [2], but now God numbers them in another way: “Therefore will I number you to the sword...” (Isa 65:12), and they brought David another number, which was to his confusion and not to his delight, for he counted those who perished by the sword of the angel, the black document of death, which was a blow to the register of David’s soldiers.
The commission of sin drags behind it a series of grave consequences; 70,000 people were killed before the plague ceased.
Often the community suffers because of the leader’s error, but on the Day of the Lord every person will be judged for his own personal error.
Perhaps someone may ask why God permitted the death of seventy thousand of the people because of David’s sin?

St. Jerome says that a person often wonders why God permitted the destruction of seventy thousand men because of the error of one man, David? And why did He permit the destruction of many because of the error of Achan the son of Carmi (Josh 7)? And why did the Lord Christ delay His coming for the salvation of the world? And so on. He answers that we try to defend God and justify His actions, but who is man that he should comprehend the wisdom of God and His plan: [Leave to God’s authority the sovereignty over your own authority, for He has no need of you to justify His actions [9].]

St. Ambrose presents us with many questions concerning the judgments of God. It is hard for man to comprehend God’s plan, because His judgments are loftier than ours. He says: [Will you too condescend...? Let God have His authority over what is His. He has no need of you to justify His works [10].]

v In truth I have already said that the crime of one person was the cause of the destruction of many of God’s people, just as the people were shattered because of the theft of Achan (Josh 7), and the plague that came because of the envy of King Saul(**), as death came because of the numbering of the people by the saint David (1 Sam 14; 1 Chr 21).

The Church of God is like the eye, and just as a speck of dirt, however small, when it falls on the eye may harm the sight, so in the same way, if some commit unclean deeds, however few they may be in the body of the Church, they hinder the radiant light of the Church [11].
Salvian, priest of Marseilles [12]

entries.section: 4. The pestilence and the deliverance of Jerusalem from it

paragraphs.text: And God sent an angel unto Jerusalem to destroy it: and as he was destroying, the LORD beheld, and he repented him of the evil, and said to the angel that destroyed, “It is enough, stay now thine hand.”
And the angel of the LORD stood by the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite. [15]

Here we see the end of the matter, for as soon as David repented, his peace with God returned to him: [O LORD, I will praise thee: though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away] (Isa 12:1). The Lord set a limit to the advance of destruction [15], and when David repented of this sin, the Lord repented of the evil sentence and commanded the destroying angel to stay his hand and return his sword to its sheath [27]. The sword of judgment was returned to its sheath, but at Calvary the sword pierced the side of our Lord Jesus Christ, and as one student said: “I entered into the heart of God through the wound of a spear.”

entries.section: 4. The pestilence and the deliverance of Jerusalem from it

paragraphs.text: And David lifted up his eyes, and saw the angel of the LORD stand between the earth and the heaven, having a drawn sword in his hand stretched out over Jerusalem.
Then David and the elders of Israel, who were clothed in sackcloth, fell upon their faces. [16]

David saw the destroying angel with his sword stretched out over Jerusalem [16], and this caused him great terror, because it was a sign of the wrath of heaven and a threat of destroying that beloved city. If the sight of an angel coming on a peaceful mission has made the greatest of men tremble, how much more the sight of an angel with a drawn sword in his hand, a fiery sword like that of the cherubim which turned every way to keep the way of the tree of life. When we are under God’s wrath, the pure angels who rejoice over a repentant sinner are against us, but we do not see them as David saw.

entries.section: 4. The pestilence and the deliverance of Jerusalem from it

paragraphs.text: And David said unto God, “Is it not I that commanded the people to be numbered?
even I it is that have sinned and done evil indeed;
but as for these sheep, what have they done?
let thine hand, I pray thee, O LORD my God, be on me, and on my father’s house; but not on thy people, that they should be plagued.” [17]

By David’s saying this to God, he presents a practical example of love with humility. In his discourse on release from death, St. Ambrose presented to us the petition of David the prophet to God that His hand be on him and on his father’s house, and not on the people, as a practical example of accepting death as a chastisement for the release of the soul from sin.

v Since the Apostle teaches us that the person who departs from his body is with Christ, provided he is worthy of this, let us contemplate the nature of life and death. We know from the teaching of Holy Scripture that death is the release of the soul from the body, a kind of separation in man. For we are freed from this bond between soul and body when we depart...
He (David) offered himself to death to atone for his disobedience to the Lord, and offered himself ready to bear the vengeance of God for the sake of the rest of his suffering people.

He knew that he would be more glorious when he died for the sake of Christ than when he reigned in this world (as a king), for what is greater than that a man should become an offering for the sake of Christ? [13]

St. Ambrose wrote St. Ambrose in his letter to the Emperor Theodosius, encouraging him to repent of what he had committed in the massacre of Thessalonica about the year 390 A.D., and asks him to imitate King David, who sinned, but offered repentance for what he had done.

David accepted the punishment for his iniquity: “let thine hand be on me, and on my father’s house” [17] [I place myself under the rod of chastisement, so let me suffer alone, for I am the one who sinned and did evil, and I am the guilty head against which the sword must be drawn].

He cast himself on God’s mercy, although he knew that God was angry with him, and no evil thought against God came to his mind, for whatever happens, “let me fall now into the hand of the LORD; for very great are his mercies” [13]. For the good man thinks well of God even if the world frowns in his face: [Though He lead me to the slaughter, I trust in Him].
He showed tender feeling and concern for his people, and his heart was pricked when he saw them smitten because of his transgression: “but as for these sheep, what have they done?” [17].
It was not easy for David to see the angel of the Lord drawing his sword against his people who were beloved to him, and against the city of Jerusalem, which had its special place in his heart.
David’s attitude was as follows:
a. He confessed his sin and asked the Lord with all his heart for pardon [8]. He confessed that he had acted foolishly and had made himself a fool.
b. He accepted chastisement from God’s hand for his sin [17], with all submission.
c. He cast himself on God’s mercy although he knew that God was angry with him [13].
d. He showed tenderness toward his people, and suffered exceedingly when he realized that what had befallen his people was because of his sin.

We are not surprised if God permits the chastisement of many because of a sin committed by a very few, perhaps by one person. For God wants His Church to be holy and without blemish. He permits temporary collective chastisement, because on the great Day of the Lord, each one will give an account of his own personal work. But here the general chastisement is permitted by the Lord as a practical sermon to all.

Pope Gregory (the Great) [14] sees that the characters of leaders are tied to the condition of those subject to them. They are often good people, but unfortunately they change because of the authority given to them. As Samuel the prophet said to King Saul that the Lord says to him: “When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel, and the LORD anointed thee king over Israel?” (1 Sam 15:17).

v David tended his father’s flock, and was taken from the flock to shepherd his people. “So he fed them according to the integrity of his heart; and guided them by the skilfulness of his hands” (Ps 78:72). And when David numbered his flock, wrath came upon them, and they began to perish. Then David surrendered himself to be accountable for his flock when he prayed, saying: [Lo, I have sinned, and I have done wickedly: but these sheep, what have they done? let thine hand, I pray thee, be against me, and against my father’s house] (2 Sam 24:17).
So also all watchful shepherds are accustomed to give themselves up on behalf of their flock [15].

St. Aphrahat v Good is humility. It saves those in danger and raises up the fallen. Humility was known from the one who said: “Lo, I have sinned, and I have done wickedly: but these sheep, what have they done? let thine hand, I pray thee, be against me, and against my father’s house” (see 2 Sam 24:17; 1 Chr 21:17). Well does David say this, he who made his kingdom subject to God, and offered repentance, and confessed his sin, and asked for pardon. He obtained salvation by humility!
Christ Himself was humble, and whoever follows the humility of Christ finds rest in Christ [16].

v So by his humility (David) became more acceptable to God, for it is not strange that the people should err, but they are blamed if they do not realize that they have sinned and so do not humble themselves before God [17].

St. Ambrose v What do you say of David, who received a great testimony from God, for He said of him: [I have found a man after mine own heart, David the son of Jesse; with my holy oil have I anointed him] (Ps 89:21).
This very man says to God: [Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions] (Ps 51:1-17).
Wash me thoroughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.
Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest.
Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.
Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom.
Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.
Make me to hear joy and gladness; that the bones which thou hast broken may rejoice.
Hide thy face from my sins, and blot out all mine iniquities.
Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
Cast me not away from thy presence; and take not thy holy spirit from me.
Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free (leading) spirit.

Then will I teach transgressors thy ways; and sinners shall be converted unto thee. Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: and my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness.
O Lord, open thou my lips; and my mouth shall shew forth thy praise.
For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering.

paragraphs.text: The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise [18].
St. Clement of Rome

entries.section: 5. The building of an altar at the threshingfloor of Ornan

paragraphs.text: 18 Then the angel of the LORD commanded Gad to say to David, that David should go up, and set up an altar unto the LORD in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite. 19 And David went up at the saying of Gad, which he spake in the name of the LORD. 20 And Ornan turned back, and saw the angel; and his four sons with him hid themselves. Now Ornan was threshing wheat. 21 And as David came to Ornan, Ornan looked and saw David, and went out of the threshingfloor, and bowed himself to David with his face to the ground. 22 Then David said to Ornan, “Grant me the place of this threshingfloor, that I may build an altar therein unto the LORD: thou shalt grant it me for the full price: that the plague may be stayed from the people.” 23 And Ornan said unto David, “Take it to thee, and let my lord the king do that which is good in his eyes: lo, I give thee the oxen also for burnt offerings, and the threshing instruments for wood, and the wheat for the meat offering; I give it all.” 24 And king David said to Ornan, “Nay; but I will verily buy it for the full price: for I will not take that which is thine for the LORD, nor offer burnt offerings without cost.” 25 So David gave to Ornan for the place six hundred shekels of gold by weight. 26 And David built there an altar unto the LORD, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and called upon the LORD; and he answered him from heaven by fire upon the altar of burnt offering. 27 And the LORD commanded the angel; and he put up his sword again into the sheath thereof. 28 At that time when David saw that the LORD had answered him in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite, then he sacrificed there. 29 For the tabernacle of the LORD, which Moses made in the wilderness, and the altar of the burnt offering, were at that season in the high place at Gibeon. 30 But David could not go before it to enquire of God: for he was afraid because of the sword of the angel of the LORD.
Then the angel of the LORD commanded Gad to say to David, that David should go up, and set up an altar unto the LORD in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite. [18]

Instructions were given to David to build an altar to the Lord at the threshingfloor of Ornan [18], and the angel commanded Gad the prophet to bring these instructions to David. The very angel who carried out the war in the name of the Lord here brings the step leading to peace. For the angels do not want us to grieve.
The angel could have brought these instructions to David directly, but he brought them through the seer, in order to show the honor of the prophets.
Likewise the Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave to John the Apostle by the hand of an angel, and from him to the churches.
The instructions to David to set up the altar were a blessed symbol of reconciliation, for if God had been pleased with his death, He would not have accepted the sacrifice from his hands.
On the mount of the mirrors, grace met righteousness.

entries.section: 5. The building of an altar at the threshingfloor of Ornan

paragraphs.text: v Observe, brethren, that there is no place in the land of the Jews worthy for the temple of the Lord to be built in it, but in the land of the Gentiles there is a chosen place; where the angel was seen, the altar was built, and by this the wrath of the Lord was appeased. This signifies that the hearts of the Jews were not found qualified for sacrifices to be offered in them, but the land of the Gentiles, that is, the conscience of Christians, is chosen as the place for the temple of the Lord. This is what the Apostle clearly indicates when he rebuked the Jews, saying: “It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you: but seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46)... This is the reason the angel of the Lord stood at the threshingfloor of the Gentile king, for the true Angel, Christ, visited the Gentile peoples [19].

entries.section: 5. The building of an altar at the threshingfloor of Ornan

paragraphs.text: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles v Here too the angel held his sword, and while he was destroying the whole city of the wicked, he pointed to the temple of the Lord at the threshingfloor of Ornan, king of the Jebusites. Thus he showed beforehand that the Church of Christ grows not in Israel, but among the Gentiles [20].
St. Jerome

entries.section: 5. The building of an altar at the threshingfloor of Ornan

paragraphs.text: And David went up at the saying of Gad, which he spake in the name of the LORD. [19]

entries.section: 5. The building of an altar at the threshingfloor of Ornan

paragraphs.text: And Ornan turned back, and saw the angel;
and his four sons with him hid themselves. Now Ornan was threshing wheat. [20]

David hastened to make an agreement with Ornan for the threshingfloor because he does not serve God at the expense of others, although Ornan offered it to him freely, not only out of kindness toward the king, but because he saw the angel [20], which aroused terror in him and his four sons, and they all hid themselves. For they could not bear the splendor of his glory, and they feared his drawn sword. His fear of the evil to come made him ready to do anything for the sake of atonement, for all who have a keen sense of the fear of God promote repentance, and encourage every way of reconciliation for the turning back of God’s wrath.

lo, I give thee the oxen also for burnt offerings, and the threshing instruments for wood, and the wheat for the meat offering;

entries.section: 5. The building of an altar at the threshingfloor of Ornan

paragraphs.text: And king David said to Ornan, “Nay; but I will verily buy it for the full price: for I will not take that which is thine for the LORD, nor offer burnt offerings without cost.” [24]

The burnt offering here means offering the whole heart to God, and also offering time or money or what we possess. Therefore David wanted to offer everything from his own money, and not from the money of others.

v Araunah offered to the blessed David the threshingfloor and the ox as a burnt sacrifice, but King David refused to accept them unless he first paid the price. This too was fulfilled at the coming of our Lord and Savior, for He refused to take the hearts of the Gentiles for Himself unless He paid His precious blood for them [21], Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles

entries.section: 5. The building of an altar at the threshingfloor of Ornan

paragraphs.text: So David gave to Ornan for the place six hundred shekels of gold by weight. [25]

The Book of Samuel mentions that the price of the oxen and the threshingfloor was very small, so David paid 50 shekels of silver (2 Sam 24:24), but the Book of Chronicles here makes clear that David bought the whole place (Hebrew hammaqom), which includes the entire area of Mount Moriah, so he paid 600 shekels of gold.
The purchase of this large area may have come at a later stage, after the purchase of the threshingfloor of wheat and the oxen that David used in the first sacrifice.

Perhaps the difference between the first and second purchase explains to us why Araunah offered at the outset to give David the threshingfloor of wheat. For it is hard to suppose that he was in a position that allowed him to give the whole of Mount Moriah, but he gives the threshingfloor only.

entries.section: 5. The building of an altar at the threshingfloor of Ornan

paragraphs.text: And David built there an altar unto the LORD, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and called upon the LORD; and he answered him from heaven by fire upon the altar of burnt offering. [26]
King David refused to take the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite to set up an altar on it freely, for he does not offer to the Lord what belongs to the money of others.

God showed His acceptance of David’s offerings on this altar, “and he answered him from heaven by fire” [26]. The proof that God’s wrath had been lifted from him is that instead of the fire justly settling on the sinner, it settled on the sacrifice and consumed it, and this was followed by the returning of the destroying sword to its sheath. Likewise Christ was made sin and a curse for us, for it pleased the Lord to bruise Him, so that God might be to us through Him not a consuming fire but a reconciled Father.

entries.section: 5. The building of an altar at the threshingfloor of Ornan

paragraphs.text: And the LORD commanded the angel; and he put up his sword again into the sheath thereof. [27]

entries.section: 5. The building of an altar at the threshingfloor of Ornan

paragraphs.text: At that time when David saw that the LORD had answered him in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite, then he sacrificed there. [28]

entries.section: 5. The building of an altar at the threshingfloor of Ornan

paragraphs.text: David continued offering his sacrifices on this altar, for the bronze altar that Moses had made was at that time in the high place at Gibeon [29], and Israel’s sacrifices were offered there. But David was afraid because of seeing the sword of the angel, so that he could not go to Gibeon to enquire of God [30], for the matter called for haste when the pestilence began. Aaron had to hasten, indeed run, to make atonement (Num 16:46-47). And the situation here was no less urgent, for time did not allow David, lest the fatal blow come before his return. Therefore God commanded him, out of pity for him, to set up an altar in that place, and God granted him a dispensation from His own law concerning the one altar because of the present trial, and permitted sacrifices to be offered on this altar, which was not set up in opposition to the one at Gibeon but alongside it, for the emblems of unity were not barred any more than unity itself, and even after the present trial had passed (as is apparent) David continued to offer sacrifices here although the altar at Gibeon continued, because God approved the sacrifices offered on the altar at the threshingfloor of Ornan and confirmed His acceptance of them [28].

entries.section: 5. The building of an altar at the threshingfloor of Ornan

paragraphs.text: For the tabernacle of the LORD, which Moses made in the wilderness, and the altar of the burnt offering, were at that season in the high place at Gibeon. [29]

God chose the site of the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite on Mount Moriah, the place where God commanded Abraham to offer his son as a sacrifice, looking forward to the time of the sacrifices of the temple, and finally the sacrifice of the Lamb of God who taketh away the sin of the world. So David built this altar where the temple would be built and sacrifice would be offered, and this is the place where God meets with His people, and it has now become the place of sacrifice.

David set up this altar, and offered a burnt sacrifice, which points to the person of Christ, and then offered a peace offering, and this also points to Christ our peace. For Christ made peace by the shedding of His blood on the Cross, and He is our peace, and it is He whose blood was sprinkled on the mercy seat for us. And He is our great High Priest, and He ascended into the heavens and is seated at the right hand of the Father, for there is no access to the Father except through our Lord Jesus Christ, the Mediator of the covenant. David realized this by the spirit of prophecies, and offered the burnt sacrifice and the peace offering to God.

entries.section: 5. The building of an altar at the threshingfloor of Ornan

paragraphs.text: But David could not go before it to enquire of God: for he was afraid because of the sword of the angel of the LORD. [30]

These two verses [29-30] explain the reason for transferring that worship to Jerusalem from Gibeon, where the tabernacle was, before which they used to enquire of the Lord (1 Chr 16:39-40; Ex 29:42) [22].
What concerns the writer here is that this trial is connected with the choice of the site of the temple that Solomon the son of David would build (1 Chr 21:18; 2 Chr 1; Gen 22:2).
Lead us not into temptation
v My God, my soul trembles lest it fall into weakness!
David, who walked after Your heart, was deceived by Satan, so he ignored for a time Your care for him, and sent the commander of his army to number those able to go to war!
Had he forgotten the day he stood before Goliath the giant, a boy carrying nothing but a sling?!
Keep me from the thoughts of the devil and his deceptions.
Protect me by Your grace, that I may not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.
v David could not bear to see his people destroyed because of his sin.
From the depths of his heart he asked that the punishment fall on him and on his father’s house.
You looked upon the cries of his heart and his tears.
You gazed upon his heart, which loved his people more than he loved himself and his father’s house.
Give me the heart of David and a double portion of his spirit!
I do not ask selfishly for myself and my family, but I ask for all the people, indeed for all mankind.
Gladden my heart with the salvation of many.
When shall I accompany You in Your love for mankind?
Then I will look continually upon Your Cross.
And I will wait in hope for the earth and the fulness thereof to become Yours, O Savior of the world!

entries.section: 1. The porters, or guards of the temple

paragraphs.text: 1 Concerning the divisions of the porters: Of the Korhites was Meshelemiah the son of Kore, of the sons of Asaph. 2 And the sons of Meshelemiah were, Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael the second, Zebadiah the third, Jathniel the fourth, 3 Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, Elioenai the seventh. 4 Moreover the sons of Obed-edom were, Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, and Sacar the fourth, and Nethaneel the fifth, 5 Ammiel the sixth, Issachar the seventh, Peulthai the eighth: for God blessed him. 6 Also unto Shemaiah his son were sons born, that ruled throughout the house of their father: for they were mighty men of valour. 7 The sons of Shemaiah; Othni, and Rephael, and Obed, Elzabad, whose brethren were strong men, Elihu, and Semachiah. 8 All these of the sons of Obed-edom: they and their sons and their brethren, able men for strength for the service, were threescore and two of Obed-edom. 9 And Meshelemiah had sons and brethren, strong men, eighteen. 10 Also Hosah, of the children of Merari, had sons; Simri the chief, (for though he was not the firstborn, yet his father made him the chief;) 11 Hilkiah the second, Tebaliah the third, Zechariah the fourth: all the sons and brethren of Hosah were thirteen. 12 Among these were the divisions of the porters, even among the chief men, having wards one against another, to minister in the house of the LORD. 13 And they cast lots, as well the small as the great, according to the house of their fathers, for every gate. 14 And the lot eastward fell to Shelemiah. Then for Zechariah his son, a wise counsellor, they cast lots; and his lot came out northward. 15 To Obed-edom southward; and to his sons the house of Asuppim. 16 To Shuppim and Hosah the lot came forth westward, with the gate Shallecheth, by the causeway of the going up, ward against ward. 17 Eastward were six Levites, northward four a day, southward four a day, and toward Asuppim two and two. 18 At Parbar westward, four at the causeway, and two at Parbar. 19 These are the divisions of the porters among the sons of Kore, and among the sons of Merari.

Great buildings must be guarded, especially the temple with all its resources and its gold and silver furnishings and the gifts generously offered to it, especially after the return from the captivity. Here he speaks of the guards or porters as a group of the Levites (see 1 Chr 9:17-27), since they play a vital role in worship; for they keep the temple from the entrance of everything unfit for the holiness of the house of the Lord, besides their watchful guarding, while keeping the doors open for the priests to enter.

The porters had their important role, and they had to bear characteristics or qualities like those of the priests (1 Chr 9:13). It is fitting for them to be marked by humility and self-denial, together with holy zeal, and courage together with strength.

Their work does not stop at guarding, for the Psalms bear witness to their work in the temple as a kind of worship. As an example it is written in the Psalm: [Lift up your heads, O ye gates; and be ye lift up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in...] (Ps 24:7 etc.).
Concerning the divisions of the porters: Of the Korhites was
Meshelemiah the son of Kore, of the sons of Asaph. [1]

The list given here of the porters is the most detailed of the three lists of the porters (1 Chr 9:17-27; 16:36-42). There were four thousand guards of the temple (1 Chr 23:4-5). They were called porters, all of them Levites. Some may think that the work of the porters is lowly and of no value; yet the porters in the service of the temple have their vital role. For they carry out many other works, among them: 1. Guarding the entrances of the temple and all the roads leading to the temple. They are responsible for the sanctity of the temple, and they do not allow anything to enter that would defile the temple. 2. Opening and closing all the outer doors and watching over them, not only on official occasions, but also in the service, in order to direct those entering for worship in the courts of the sanctuary with due propriety, and to encourage the penitents, and to turn away strangers and the unclean, and to guard the temple from thieves and others who are enemies of the house of God; and in this there is a hint of the priests of the New Testament, who were entrusted with the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven, to bind and to loose according to the law of the Lord Christ (Mt 16:19). 3. Examining the tools and vessels that were used every day, and making sure they were returned to their places. 4. Taking care of the furnishings of the temple and doing the cleaning work, and preparing the offerings for the sacrifices. 5. Mixing the incense that was burned daily.

The first guard that Holy Scripture records for us took place after the fall of Adam, for it is said: “So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life” (Gen 3:24).

If the temple of Solomon needed strict guarding to keep anything unclean from entering it, then there must be no laxity concerning the holiness of the Church of the Lord Christ, who redeemed her with His precious blood, and sent to her His Holy Spirit that she may be sanctified and prepared for the heavenly wedding! And the believer, as a member of the holy Church, since he carries treasures in his depths, needs strict heavenly guarding. Therefore he cries out every morning, saying: “Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips” (Ps 141:3).

The godly Levites can guard the doors of the temple and its treasures and keep it clean, but who can guard my inner mouth and the senses of my soul and cleanse my depths from every sin except You? My depths cry out: “Except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Ps 127:1). You alone have established Your kingdom in me, and made me a temple for You; O Lord, arise to guard me, for I am Yours, and the enemy of good does not cease attacking me and plundering Your treasures from within me!

v We must bridle the tongue, so that it does not run to excess in the folly of speech. And when it speaks to profit, then it ought not to be silent through sloth. The prophet contemplated this matter and said: “Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips” (Ps 141:3). Here the psalmist did not ask the Lord to set a fence or a wall, but a door that can be opened or closed. Let us learn when to open our mouths wisely and at the proper time, and, on the contrary, how to close them with silence [1].
Father Gregory (the Great)

paragraphs.text: 20 And of the Levites, Ahijah was over the treasures of the house of God, and over the treasures of the dedicated things. 21 As concerning the sons of Laadan; the sons of the Gershonite Laadan, chief fathers, even of Laadan the Gershonite, were Jehieli. 22 The sons of Jehieli; Zetham, and Joel his brother, which were over the treasures of the house of the LORD. 23 Of the Amramites, and the Izharites, the Hebronites, and the Uzzielites: 24 And Shebuel the son of Gershom, the son of Moses, was ruler of the treasures. 25 And his brethren by Eliezer; Rehabiah his son, and Jeshaiah his son, and Joram his son, and Zichri his son, and Shelomith his son. 26 Which Shelomith and his brethren were over all the treasures of the dedicated things, which David the king, and the chief fathers, the captains over thousands and hundreds, and the captains of the host, had dedicated. 27 Out of the spoils won in battles did they dedicate to maintain the house of the LORD. 28 And all that Samuel the seer, and Saul the son of Kish, and Abner the son of Ner, and Joab the son of Zeruiah, had dedicated; and whosoever had dedicated any thing, it was under the hand of Shelomith, and of his brethren.
And of the Levites, Ahijah was over the treasures of the house of God, and over the treasures of the dedicated things. [20]

Some of the Levites were appointed to guard the treasures of the temple and the spoils and the freewill offerings. They also supervise the preparation of the sacrifices and their preservation, and keep the accounts of the gifts offered.

They keep the treasures so that neither rust nor moth corrupts them and thieves do not break in and steal, and they spend from them as needed without extravagance or reduction or squandering, and perhaps they recorded what came in and went out.

There were treasures of the house of God, for the house was great and could not be managed without various treasuries. Much of the flour for the altar and wine and oil and salt and fuel, besides the lamps, was spent daily, so quantities like these were stored up beforehand, in addition to the garments and the holy vessels; these were the storehouses of the house of God. And since money is needed to buy everything, without doubt much of it came from the offerings of the people, and perhaps much of it was set aside for necessity, and these treasuries signify the abundance in the house of the heavenly Father, for in it there is sufficiency and more than enough; for in Christ (the true temple) are the treasures of wisdom and knowledge and unsearchable riches.

Afterward this blessed custom was revived, and not only Samuel and David, but also Abner and Joab dedicated from their spoils to maintain the house of the Lord [28], for in works of righteousness and goodness God expects from us much of what He bestows upon us, for great success calls for a corresponding return.

The last chapter of (1 Chr 26) speaks of the role of the Levites in their relation to the people, for some of them were appointed as public officials to serve the people and the king, and also to carry out other official works, and to collect the temple’s share from them, together with attention to the ministry of teaching. entries.section: 3. The officers and judges

paragraphs.text: 107 thousand were appointed to work west of the Jordan River, and 2700 to work on the eastern side of the Jordan in Gilead. They are put in charge of every matter pertaining to God and the affairs of the king [32]. They received special distinction, and were in contact with King David.

God’s purpose at first was that Israel should be a theocratic nation ruled by God. The tabernacle of the congregation was in the midst of the people, and the priests derived their decisions from God. But this changed because of the failure of the Levites, so God raised up judges for them. But the people asked for a king, and this led to David now being on the throne, and although the state of Israel had become a monarchy, David concentrated on bringing it back under the authority of God.
Of the Izharites, Chenaniah and his sons were for the outward business over Israel, for officers and judges [29]

Here we see an account of those who were employed as officers and judges for the outward business, which must not be neglected, for rulers are appointed by God for the benefit of the Church, as are the ministers also.

The Levites were employed in the administration of justice alongside the leaders and heads of the tribes because of their knowledge of the laws more than anyone else, for this was the subject of their study.

paragraphs.text: And of the Hebronites, Hashabiah and his brethren, men of valour, a thousand and seven hundred, were officers among them of Israel on this side Jordan westward in all the business of the LORD, and in the service of the king. [30]

Their task was in all the business of the LORD and the service of the king [30, 32], so they managed the affairs of the country both ecclesiastically and civilly, such as God’s tithes and the king’s taxes, and punishing crimes committed against God and His honor or against the government and the peace of the people, and guarding against idolatry and acts of injustice and carrying out the laws concerning them. It is probable that some of them took care of religious matters, and others of civil matters, and by their cooperation together good service was rendered to God and the king.

paragraphs.text: 1 Now the children of Israel after their number, to wit, the chief fathers and captains of thousands and hundreds, and their officers that served the king in any matter of the courses, which came in and went out month by month throughout all the months of the year, of every course were twenty and four thousand. 2 Over the first course for the first month was Jashobeam the Jehoiada, a chief priest: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 6 This is that Benaiah, who was mighty among the thirty, and above the thirty: and in his course was Ammizabad his son. 7 The fourth captain for the fourth month was Asahel the brother of Joab, and Zebadiah his son after him: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 8 The fifth captain for the fifth month was Shamhuth the Izrahite: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 9 The sixth captain for the sixth month was Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 10 The seventh captain for the seventh month was Helez the Pelonite, of the children of Ephraim: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 11 The eighth captain for the eighth month was Sibbecai the Hushathite, of the Zarhites: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 12 The ninth captain for the ninth month was Abiezer the Anetothite, of the Benjamites: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 13 The tenth captain for the tenth month was Maharai the Netophathite, of the Zarhites: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 14 The eleventh captain for the eleventh month was Benaiah the Pirathonite, of the children of Ephraim: and in his course were twenty and four thousand. 15 The twelfth captain for the twelfth month was Heldai the Netophathite, of Othniel: and in his course were twenty and four thousand.

Now the children of Israel after their number, to wit, the chief fathers and captains of thousands and hundreds, and their officers that served the king in any matter of the courses, which came in and went out month by month throughout all the months of the year, of every course were twenty and four thousand. [1]

Here we find an account of the organization of the divisions of the kingdom’s army. David himself was a man of war, and did great deeds with the sword, and brought down many armies into battle, and now he organizes them after God has given him rest from his enemies. He did not gather them all together, because that might cause hardship to them and to the state; yet he did not disband them or scatter them all, because that might leave the kingdom in danger, and the people might forget the art of war which they had learned. Therefore he planned to keep a permanent force, but not a standing army. 1. He kept 240,000 armed men continually, perhaps as one organized division in one place in the kingdom. This force was sufficient to preserve safety and peace for the people, and we as true Christians must learn spiritual warfare, because we have spiritual enemies and we must take care to stand always against them. 2. He changed them every month, and thus the total of the militia was 288,000, perhaps a fifth of the able men of the kingdom, and by distributing them into 12 divisions they were educated and trained in military matters, yet no one was obliged to serve more than one month in the year at his own expense, and surely this was within their ability, except in emergencies, when it was easy for them to be gathered together quickly. This is part of the wisdom of leaders, that while they provide security for the people, they plan for this to be done in an easy and effective way and, as far as possible, as less of a burden on the people. 3. Each division had a chief captain besides the captains of thousands and hundreds, and these twelve are mentioned among David’s mighty men in (2 Sam 23; 1 Chr 11).
“The chief fathers” or “the heads of the fathers’ houses” are individuals or households who rendered regular service to King David with the materials needed for establishing the temple.
“Twenty and four thousand”: Some see that the number thousand does not mean an arithmetical thousand, but is an expression used to mean a division or battalion of whatever number.

paragraphs.text: This is that Benaiah, who was mighty among the thirty, and above the thirty: and in his course was Ammizabad his son. [6]

Benaiah’s son was in his division [6], and Asahel’s son was after him [7]. From this it appears that the organization of the militia was established at the beginning of David’s reign, because Asahel was killed by Abner while David was reigning in Hebron, and he renewed this method after he had finished his wars and put military affairs in this position as a preparation for peace in the reign of Solomon; so when we think that we are safe as long as we are in the body, we must be ready for spiritual wars.

There was a common saying in the East that carried a meaning, which kings sent to their enemies, that it is not fitting for one who puts on arms to boast like one who has gone to the battle and returned victorious. He must conquer and achieve victory, and then he may boast of his victory. A man ought not to boast beforehand of what will happen, for he knows not what a day may bring forth (Prov 27:1). Let him wait until the battle is finished, for “Let not him that girdeth on his harness boast himself as he that putteth it off” (1 Kgs 20:11). The Apostle says: “Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor 10:12).

v Our standing here is not a safe standing. No, not until we are delivered from the currents of this present life and sail to the quiet harbor. Do not then be puffed up that you stand, but take heed lest you fall; for if Paul feared this, and he was more steadfast than all of us, how much more is it fitting for us to be on our guard?! [1]
v He who reviles others falls at once into the same sins. Therefore the blessed Paul counsels us: “Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” [2].

v The first feature of the organization of military forces (military tactics) is to know how to stand well. Many things depend on this. Therefore he often speaks of standing firm, saying: “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith” (1 Cor 16:13). And also: “stand fast... in the Lord” (Phil 4:1), and also: “Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.” And also: “and having done all, to stand” (Eph 6:13). Without doubt he does not mean just any way of standing, but the right way, and as many who have experience in wars know the utmost importance of knowing how to stand. If in the case of boxers and wrestlers the trainers mention this matter before everything, I mean standing firm, how much more must it have priority in wars and military affairs [3].
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 2. The heads of the tribes of Israel

paragraphs.text: 16 Furthermore over the tribes of Israel: the ruler of the Reubenites was Eliezer the son of Zichri: of the Simeonites, Shephatiah the son of Maachah: 17 Of the Levites, Hashabiah the son of Kemuel: of the Aaronites, Zadok: 18 Of Judah, Elihu, one of the brethren of David: of Issachar, Omri the son of Michael: 19 Of Zebulun, Ishmaiah the son of Obadiah: of Naphtali, Jerimoth the son of Azriel: 20 Of the children of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Azaziah: of the half tribe of Manasseh, Joel the son of Pedaiah: 21 Of the half tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, Iddo the son of Zechariah: of Benjamin, Jaasiel the son of Abner: 22 Of Dan, Azareel the son of Jeroham. These were the princes of the tribes of Israel. 23 But David took not the number of them from twenty years old and under: because the LORD had said he would increase Israel like to the stars of the heavens. 24 Joab the son of Zeruiah began to number, but he finished not, because there fell wrath for it against Israel; neither was the number put in the account of the chronicles of king David.
Furthermore over the tribes of Israel: the ruler of the Reubenites was Eliezer the son of Zichri:
of the Simeonites, Shephatiah the son of Maachah. [16]

They still kept the order that Moses had arranged long ago in the wilderness, that each tribe must have a leader or chief, and it probably continued either by election or by succession in the same family, and those mentioned here are those who were found when these events were recounted; for Elihu or Eliab, who was chief of Judah, was the eldest son of Jesse, who came from the line of Nahshon and Salmon, who were chiefs of the tribe in the days of Moses, and we suppose that their authority was now less than it was when each tribe acted on its own, for now all the tribes are subject not only to the king alone, but also to the chief of the tribe.
Our Christianity urges us to submit not only to the king as supreme, but also to governors sent by him (1 Pet 2:13-14) for the execution of justice.
The list of the tribes came arranged in a certain order.
First the sons of Leah in a suitable order: the Reubenites, the Simeonites, the Levites, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun.
After that the sons of Rachel: Joseph represented by his two sons Ephraim and Manasseh; then Benjamin.
The sons of Bilhah: given not in chronological order: Naphtali and Dan.
The sons of Zilpah: Gad and Asher are not mentioned here.

The names of the heads of the tribes of Israel in the days of David indicate the existence of cooperation, ease and stability between the king and the heads of the old tribes, unlike what happened in the days of Solomon, when a kind of dispute was found that appeared clearly immediately after Solomon’s death.
