From the tribe of Benjamin the chief was Jaasiel the son of Abner, and although Abner was an enemy of David and opposed his ascending the throne, David did not oppose this promotion, but perhaps himself recommended him for this high post, and this teaches us to repay evil with good. A wonderful picture of the person of David, who practiced the commandment of the Gospel while under the Law!

v No one can love his enemies, or do good to those who hate him, or suffer for those who wrong him. But if he remembers the human nature common to them, he does not mind the sufferings they cause him, and the more cruel they are to him, the more he is gentle with them. A father grieves and is saddened over his deranged son all the more as the son’s madness and violence increase.
Paul diagnosed the disease that causes those fierce attacks against him, so his concern for them and his care for them as sick people increased.

We hear him addressing us with exceeding kindness and tenderness about those who scourged him five times (2 Cor 24:11), and stoned him and bound him and shed his blood and desired to cut him in pieces, and he says of them: “For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 2:10). And he also pressed hard on those who wrong them, saying: “Be not highminded, but fear: for if God spared not the natural branches, take heed lest he also spare not thee” (Rom 20:11, 21). And when he saw the judgment falling upon them, he could do nothing but what he was able to do, which was that he wept and mourned for them without ceasing [4].

v When you are one with those who attack you and are mingled with them, you overcome them (by love and faith). And just as leaven hidden in dough does not perish, but rather changes the nature of the dough, so also in the preaching of the Gospel. Therefore do not be afraid when I tell you that tribulations are coming, for your light no one can extinguish, but it overcomes all men [5].
St. John Chrysostom

paragraphs.text: But David took not the number of them from twenty years old and under: because the LORD had said he would increase Israel like to the stars of the heavens. [23]

When David ordered the numbering of the people, he forbade the numbering of those under twenty years of age, and he thought by this that he would remove suspicion about what he had done with regard to the promise that they would not be numbered; but this was a weak precaution, because it was never the custom to number those under twenty, for the promise concerning their number was about men of action.

entries.section: 2. The heads of the tribes of Israel

paragraphs.text: Joab the son of Zeruiah began to number, but he finished not, because there fell wrath for it against Israel; neither was the number put in the account of the chronicles of king David. [24]
The census was not completed, because the wrath of the Lord came before Joab finished it; perhaps David was ashamed of his sin, so he asked that the records of the census not be presented publicly.
David refused to use this census, since this census was counted as a corruption that came in the age of David.

The census that David took of the people out of pride of heart was not good; it was never completed and was not done accurately, and was not recorded as a true census. For Joab was weary of it and completed it only in part, and David was ashamed of it and wished it to be forgotten, because the punishment fell on Israel on account of it, and the good man, returning to himself, cannot find pleasure in what angers God, and cannot use anything he obtained through sin. David took the census in a moment of pride and unbelief, but now he did not take a census but relied on the promises of God.
David had 12 officers in charge of local affairs. And he had counsellors and close friends who gave him counsel.

entries.section: 3. The chief civil officials

paragraphs.text: 25 And over the king’s treasures was Azmaveth the son of Adiel: and over the storehouses in the fields, in the cities, and in the villages, and in the castles, was Jehonathan the son of Uzziah: 26 And over them that did the work of the field for tillage of the ground was Ezri the son of Chelub: 27 And over the vineyards was Shimei the Ramathite: over the increase of the vineyards for the wine cellars was Zabdi the Shiphmite: 28 And over the olive trees and the sycomore trees that were in the low plains was Baal-hanan the Gederite: and over the cellars of oil was Joash: 29 And over the herds that fed in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite: and over the herds that were in the valleys was Shaphat the son of Adlai: 30 Over the camels also was Obil the Ishmaelite: and over the asses was Jehdeiah the Meronothite: 31 And over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagerite. All these were the rulers of the substance which was king David’s.

The last section of this chapter refers to the king’s possessions and sources of income that were used in his administration of the kingdom, and these multiplied during his reign. It is noticeable that in (Ezek 46:16-18), after more than four centuries, the possessions of the royal family were firmly defined.
David did not demand taxes from the people, and his hand did not extend to the spoils of war, for he left the latter for the account of the temple (1 Chr 26:26).

paragraphs.text: And over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagerite.
All these were the rulers of the substance which was king David’s. [31]

The rulers of the king’s substance, as they were called, were concerned with supervising the king’s husbandry: his vineyards, his olive trees, his herds, his camels, his asses, and his flocks. Here there are no state ministers or sports officials or masters of ceremonies, but all are in a service suited to the simplicity of those days. David was a severe soldier, and a great teacher, and a great ruler, but he was a faithful steward over his possessions. So he took much under his hand and stored it, not for pleasure but for profit, for the king himself is served by the field (Eccl 5:9). Rulers who want their subjects to be diligent must give themselves as an example in diligence and in managing affairs. But we find that afterward they made the poor of the land vinedressers and husbandmen (2 Kgs 25:12), and now David entrusted these works to his great men.

entries.section: 4. The king’s counsellors

paragraphs.text: 32 Also Jonathan David’s uncle was a counsellor, a wise man, and a scribe: and Jehiel the son of Hachmoni was with the king’s sons: 33 And Ahithophel was the king’s counsellor: and Hushai the Archite was the king’s companion: 34 And after Ahithophel was Jehoiada the son of Benaiah, and Abiathar: and the general of the king’s army was Joab.
Also Jonathan David’s uncle was a counsellor, a wise man, and a scribe:
and Jehiel the son of Hachmoni was with the king’s sons: [32]
Holy Scripture does not indicate anywhere the existence of an uncle of David serving as his counsellor, therefore some translate the word “uncle” as “the beloved.”

Those who supervised the king’s household were known for wisdom and the art of speech. His uncle was a counsellor, a wise man, and a scribe, not only an expert in politics, but learned in the Holy Scriptures, and David made him his counsellor, and another, without doubt distinguished in learning and seasoned, he made the tutor of his sons, and Ahithophel, a cunning man, was also a counsellor to David, but faithful Hushai was his friend and the keeper of his secrets. It seems that he did not have many counsellors, but those he had were marked by great abilities. The wisdom of leaders appears in the choice of their servants, and David, in spite of the trusted ones and relatives beloved to him and the counsellors around him, preferred the word of God above all (Ps 119:24): “Thy testimonies also are my delight and my counsellors.”
